speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
subtopic: MESSAGE FROM THE PRIME MINISTER TO AIR OFFICER IN CHIEF OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has been unable to come to the house to-day. In his absence I believe hon. members would wish me to read the text of the message which the Prime Minister sent this morning to the Air Officer in Chief, Royal Canadian Air Force overseas: Air Officer in Chief,
R.C.A.F. Overseas,
London.
The growing strength of the Royal Canadian Air Force overseas and the reports of its increasing share in actual combat with the enemy have filled Canada with pride. The hearts of the Canadian people have been particularly stirred by the news of the important and considerable part which Canadian airmen had in the raid on Cologne with its far-reaching effects.
On behalf of the government, I would ask you kindly to convey to the officers and airmen of the Royal Canadian Air Force under your command, and, through the appropriate channels, to the Canadian officers and airmen serving with the Royal Air Force, an expression of the pride of all Canada in their great and growing achievements. Please extend as well our best of wishes for every success in future aerial combat. The Canadian people will ever gratefully remember what the gallant young airmen of Canada are doing to defend the security of 
their homeland and to preserve freedom by engaging and occupying the enemy in the skies over Europe, and in other parts of the world.
W. L. Mackenzie King,
Prime Minister.

If the purpose of question No. 1 is to ascertain the profits of each of the chartered banks earned in Canada the answer is that the banks are not required by the Bank Act or otherwise to publish or report separately the results of their Canadian business as distinguished from their external or over-all operations. The net profits of' each of the chartered banks for the fiscal years ended in 1941 are shown in the attached statement.
While the figures submitted are compiled from the regular annual profit and loss statements of the banks, it should be pointed out that all banks do not publish such statements in precisely the same form, not being required to do so by the general terms of section 53 (8) of the Bank Act. Moreover, to arrive at true net profits on a uniform basis the figures shown in column I should properly be reduced by the respective amounts shown in column III, since appropriations to write down the cost of premises, as well as contributions to pension funds, etc., are definitely provided out of earnings, and consequently decrease the amount finally available to shareholders.
Although the percentages of profits to paid up capital only are asked for, additional calculations have been made as indicated by the statement, particular attention being drawn to the percentage realtionship of net profits (column VII) to the total of shareholders' money invested, namely, capital paid up, reserve and undivided profits. It is the percentages shown in this column which reflect for all practical purposes the real relationship of final net profits to total shareholders' investment. The percentage of profits to capital paid up alone is necessarily a nominal or arbitrary one only (although sometimes incorrectly used as a measure of earnings) as other shareholders' funds also go to constitute the entire capital owned and at risk by shareholders.

subtopic: CALLING OP MEN TO AGE THIRl'Y-PIVE-SELECTION BY LOT
speechtext:
Speaking in the house on Thursday, May 28, as reported on page 2872 of Hansard, the Minister of National War Services indicated that he would not be surprised if the age limit for men to be called up should be moved forward to thirty-five years within a very short time. The announcement that the age limit for compulsory service would be raised from twenty-four to thirty years was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on- March 24, as reported on page 1566 of Hansard. At that time the Prime Minister stated:
It has also been decided to select the men to be called up for service by drawing lots over the whole field of those who are subject to the proclamation. As soon as the necessary administrative arrangements have been worked out for this plan of selection by lot, a detailed announcement will be made by the Minister of National War Services.
I now ask the minister, first, have the available single men between twenty-four and thirty years been practically exhausted? Second, has the minister abandoned the plan of selecting men by drawing lots, or is it intended to advance the age limit and to select the men within the given ages by lot? Third, if it is still intended to use the lottery method, when will the minister make the detailed statement announced by the Prime Minister?

I want to lodge a protest with the Minister of Finance against the present method of handling the agricultural affairs of this country, if the wartime prices and trade board is under the minister's control, which I believe it is. I think it is time that the attention of the house and the country was drawn to the fact that the wartime prices and trade board is dealing with agriculture, fisheries, and many other matters, and I am going to protest as loudly as I can against the present drift. The farmers are suffering from the low prices established on agricultural products. When you go to the Department of Agriculture they say: "We have nothing to do with it; you had better go to the Department of Finance." I protest strongly on behalf of the people of this country, and particularly the farmers, who are working like slaves below the cost of production. Things are getting so involved that you do not know what department to go to. When you want to deal with fisheries matters, you are told: "Under the wartime prices and trade board." When you want to deal with agricultural prices, you are told: "Under the wartime prices and trade board." When you want to deal w'ith any matter almost, you are told: "Under the wartime prices and trade board."

I have an advertisement here-I do not know who is advising the wartime prices and trade board-telling how much sugar children should have, and it says: "Children need sugar because it helps to build energy for active little bodies." Have they a doctor in the wartime prices and trade board who is advising them on matters of this kind? I warn this house and the country that there is a dangerous drift right now, and it is time to protest and to ask the minister where we are going.

I think the protest by the hon. member for New Westminster is well founded. We have refrained from raising this question of controls because it is said to be unpatriotic to do so. That is the whole reason why this question has not been aired in parliament before now. The minister will have to say something in defence of this body that he has set up. I wish I had my files here. I could read what the minister said in this house on November 21, 1940, about price ceilings. I do not want to delay the committee, and I am not going to make a speech, but I suggest that hon. members read what the minister said in the debate on the address on November 21, 1940. I should like to quote what he said on that occasion. He

War Appropriation-Finance
condemned price control out of hand. Then, after a long time, after somebody had sold him this idea; we had a complete reversal of attitude by the minister. The people of this country are bewildered.
I am in favour of control in war time to prevent inflation, if it can be done by any kind of decent method. I think the objective is good. I am not going to condemn it. But the whole difficulty is that they froze prices in this country on an uneven structure. There is the whole story. And they did it in an effort to do two things, to prevent the cost-of-living index from rising, and to prevent wages from rising. And who is the sufferer? The primary producer is the sufferer-absolutely. The wartime prices and trade board had thought for only certain factors in this body politic. They have had thought for the consumer; and of course he is entitled to con- * sideration. But there are other people in this country besides the consumer. There is the wage earner, and above all there is the impoverished producer.
I am looking at the hon. member for Yarmouth. Go down into his community and see how the fishermen have been suffering because of the low prices of their commodities. Go into my community and see how the potato grower has been suffering, until this very year. Three years out of four he has operated at a loss, and in the fourth year, when he has a chance to recoup himself for the losses which he sustained in the three preceding years, a ceiling is placed on his product and he is told, "No; now that the opportunity is come for you to recoup yourself for the last three years you just cannot do it; you must shoulder your losses and pay them out of your capital."
This sort of thing has gone a long way, and I think it would be highly desirable to have a good wide-open discussion on it. I use a classic illustration, the question of hay. Hay is a prosaic commodity, but in the days gone by, in the Saint John valley and all across the river valleys of eastern Canada, it was a fine commodity and it sustained many a farmer. In the days of the automobile down to a comparatively recent period hay was a drug on the market. Last year it began to look up. Last year we had a good crop. What happened? When the farmers had just about completed the baling of their hay, at the period when hay is at its very lowest level of the whole year, between the 15th of September and the 11th of October, the price of baled hay was frozen. The trend of the market has always been upwards from October 1, to near the time when the new crop is in. Farmers in the Saint John river valley
had the price of one of their principal commodities frozen, and it is unjust and unfair to these producers. I raise a protest on behalf of the hay farmers of the Saint John river and of the eastern townships and every other part of Canada.
Right across Canada.

Yes, you
can see the same thing right across Canada. Here is something right under my nose, something which comes directly to my attention. It is something which many farmers are demanding to know. They are willing to make sacrifices for the war effort, but they see the huge prices which are being paid in the industrial areas; they see that 85 per cent of the increased national revenue is going to the wage earners, the consumers-and how much do these producers get? Nothing.
I think the hon. member for New Westminster deserves thanks for having raised this question. I am not going to carry it on now because I know that the minister is anxious to meet the wishes of the hon. member for Lethbridge, but this pot has been boiling a long time and somebody has to have the courage to deal with it. The whole subject has been dealt with without any plan at all; it is hit or miss, hit and run, trial and error, and the primary producer is the sufferer.

I wish to say just a word following the remarks of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson). It is to ask the minister to postpone this discussion until each member has had an opportunity of reading what the minister has produced. He is the only one who knows what is contained in the few sheets of paper he has handed to Hansard; therefore I think it would be unfair to all of us to insist that we continue the discussion now. The least that can be asked is that every hon. member should have the opportunity to read it in Hansard, and then the discussion should be much smoother; moreover, it will be orderly. At the present time, since we do not know what is before us, it is very hard for anyone to speak to the point. I hope the minister will be kind enough to appreciate this circumstance, and take up something else.
I should like to support the leader of the opposition in some of his remarks.

Hear,,
hear. A new convert 1

No, not a new convert at all, because as a matter of fact I suppose
War Appropriation-Finance

the only group in this chamber which over a period of years has urged an intelligently planned economic structure is the group with which I am associated.
Well, well, well.

That is absolutely correct. But, you cannot have economic planning simply by imposing something in an arbitrary manner, and that is precisely the defect in connection with the control of prices. I am not complaining that the government did attempt to control prices. I think it was the proper thing to do under the existing circumstances. But the unfortunate feature of the whole thing was that they adopted arbitrarily the price level of a certain period, with the result that prices and wages which were out of line were frozen at those levels.
Those of us who come from the prairies remember that within the last few months we have had a long debate regarding a price level for wheat, and the price level for wheat was raised, I believe largely because of the pressure which was brought to bear by the western farm delegations and by various discussions in this house. But although the price of wheat was raised to a degree, it still was not brought up to a parity level. While we welcome the increases which were made, nevertheless we know perfectly well that there are other producers-the fishermen were mentioned a few moments ago; the producers of hay, the producers of other commodities, and then of course you have in some instances wages entirely out of line with those which are paid in other fields of endeavour. There are still people in this country who are getting less than 35 cents an hour and whose wages are more or less frozen at that level.
I believe it would be well if parliament would consider the matter of price control in a much wider and broader manner than it has been considered hitherto. When people look around and see some of the great manufacturing concerns engaged in war work increasing their net profits by very large amounts they naturally wonder just how that can be reconciled with the fact that producers of essential commodities are compelled to accept figures which are below the cost of production. We cannot solve this problem piecemeal; we cannot solve it by arbitrarily selecting a period and imposing an arbitrary price which is thereafter to prevail. What we should do is. to endeavour to arrive at a fair basis of parity prices for at least primary and essential commodities, and then
IMr. Coldwell.]
relate to that the wage levels and so on, so that there may be a measure of justice in the imposition of a price ceiling.
I do not propose to say more at this time, but when the budget is before the house I hope the minister will make a complete statement on the price ceiling and the policy in regard to it, and that at that time we may discuss the matter with more information at our disposal, so that we may be able to arrive at a better understanding of just what is being done. I am going to state, in fairness to the minister and those who advise him, that this is an attempt at least to prevent the price level from running away with itself, thereby bringing about a chaotic inflationary situation in this country.

Following the remarks already made on this subject and the request of the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), I think the Minister of Agriculture should take some part in the discussion of this resolution. I know I have some questions I should like to ask with regard to the marketing of eggs, poultry and other agricultural products. There are some rather embarrassing matters connected with the marketing of these products which I think should be dealt with by the Minister of Agriculture under this measure.
I should like to say a word about the matter of controllers. I am satisfied that some of these controllers are given too much authority, and that they do not extend the proper cooperation to others in authority. A week or so ago I received some telegrams from my own community asking if permission could be obtained for the use of trucks to take people to certain school field days, which are held under the authority of the provincial department of education. In one of these telegrams it was pointed out that it would take ten or twelve automobiles and drivers to transport these children, while one truck and driver might be able to take them just as easily. You will realize the wastage of man-power and gasoline which could be avoided in that way. A government member from my province received a wire stating that some twenty automobiles and drivers would be required for this purpose, whereas the same number of people could be transported in one large truck. I spent most of the day with the officials concerned with this matter; I telephoned the controller in Toronto, but he refused to grant permission. The minister will realize that in the provinces we have public utility boards which have detailed information as to the operation of trucks, automobiles, buses, and so on. I suggest that the minister ask the controllers who have to do with

War Appropriation-Finance
these matters to call a meeting of representatives of these utility boards in order to get the benefit of their experience, which extends over the last ten or fifteen years. In one day they would be able to obtain a great deal of useful advice, which might be of guidance to them when they consider issuing these drastic orders. If this is not done in the very near future the minister may not receive the cooperation on the part of the public which he and the government have been receiving up to this point.
I had the privilege of returning home last week and I was amazed at the number of agricultural producers who, irrespective of politics, are thoroughly disgusted with the manner in which these orders are being issued by the various controllers. These people are willing to sacrifice everything they have to buy bonds and war savings stamps; they will do everything possible to help win the war, but they do not like the way these orders are issued. Why, farmers who do not even attempt to operate cars but who own trucks are told that they cannot use those trucks to take their families to town to do the marketing. They are told they may not use their trucks to take their families to church on Sunday, which to me seems absurd. Then recently they were told that they may write to some divisional registrar and get a permit to use their trucks in this way if their application is approved. This system of controls and controllers needs looking into. It is creating an impossible situation in this country, which may develop into a very great hindrance to the war effort. I trust the minister will take this matter into consideration and see that some check is made.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I am a little at a loss to know where we are at to-day. I understood that the Minister of Finance was going to make a statement.

The hon. member for New Westminster put his finger upon a very sore spot, the cause of which simply must be removed; and in my opinion that matter should be discussed under this two billion dollar war appropriation. To the extent to which the Minister of Finance has in any way neglected to manage the
economic affairs of Canada as they should be managed in the best interests of Canada, to that extent he is answerable to this house for the way in which he has administered his department. Therefore he should be brought to attention, shall I say, or called to account under this war appropriation.
I am particularly surprised to find that the leader of the opposition, who was so supinely willing to give up the discussion of this whole matter, apparently having concluded that it had been discussed sufficiently, should be so full of things to say even before he was in order. Now, however, all I want to do is find out whether or not the Minister of Finance is going to make a statement before we have any general discussion. I had concluded that he would, and I think it is the right way to proceed. Let the minister make, his statement, as the other ministers have done already. Then let hon. members discuss, in an orderly fashion, the various aspects of that statement.

I am sure the hon. member will not misunderstand me if I raise a point of order. On Friday afternoon the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) had almost completed his argument at six o'clock, and he would like to conclude his statement now, if the hon. member for Temiscouata does not mind.

I shall gladly agree to the suggestion of the hon. member. According to the rules I have the right to speak now, but just to show my spirit of fraternity I am delighted to give the hon. member for Cape Breton South an opportunity to conclude his remarks.

I want to thank the hon. member for Temiscouata for his cooperation; it is good to get a little from that side occasionally.
At the time of adjournment on Friday afternoon, I was endeavouring to point out that the boards now functioning for the purpose of calling men for military service would have to be reorganized if they are to do the job that has to be done. I think we gave the minister concrete evidence of that in the situation which arose in Toronto, where an important aeroplane plant was disrupted by having some four hundred of its trained men called for military service, some of whom had been declared medically unfit only a short time before. I was endeavouring, not for the purpose of criticizing but with the desire to help,

to point out that I have considerable confidence in the people who are handling the national selective service, and I suggested that if the industries which are all-important to the war effort are to be protected in future, national selective service will have to have some considerable say on the boards that are calling up men for military service.
My conception of the whole situation now is that most of the men who will be called for military service in the different age groups in the future will come from industry, perhaps from industries that are essential. In view of the definite regulations laid down to be administered by the national selective service authorities, they will have to be given some representation on these boards, and some say, because the emphasis now is not on whether a man is eligible for service but rather on how essential he may be in industry. In that connection I am wondering whether national selective service has any latitude with respect to men who may be taken from industry. When we adjourned on Friday I was pointing out that there is considerable apprehension on the part of employees in the steel industry. For example, I had a letter from the secretary of lodge No. 1064, of the steel workers' union, at Sydney, Nova Scotia, where in one plant there are some 4,000 or 5,000 employees who are members of this union. In this letter it was pointed out that at that time, May 0, it was rumoured that instructions recently had been issued to all employers to prepare to release all men between the ages of twenty-one and thirty, and in this letter the fear was expressed that if the matter were left solely to the employers it could be done in a discriminatory manner, that a company policy of favoritism could be imposed. There is every justification for that expression of fear on the part of the members of the union. It is pleasant to be charitable, to think along charitable lines and to presuppose that the other fellow is as honest and patriotic as you are. Unfortunately the experience of these unions in the past does not give them much confidence in what the companies may do. The employer now has the right to go before the board-[DOT]

It is the employee who
has the right to make the application.

But the employer has the
right to appear before the board, and he makes the decision as to whether or not the employee is essential. In an organized plant you have men who are active in the union and who consistently work toward the raising of the standard of living of the employees. As a rule men of that calibre are not very well liked by the employers; so that

War Appropriation

War Services
if one of them should be called for military service, regardless of how essential he may be to the industry it would be an easy matter for the employer to decide that he was not so essential, and to shift him out. I do not think it is asking too much on behalf of the working people to ask that labour be given representation on these boards. It must be done if they are to function properly, particularly when you have as chairman a judge who is impartial but who in most cases has not had much experience with the problems of the common people or the essentiality of men in industry.
In the west the farmers are represented on the boards. That is all to the good, since agriculture is the industiy directly affected there. In the industrial sections, where the employer has an opportunity to be called in, labour should be represented. After all we must remember that it is the employee who is being regimented. His are the liberties that are being taken away. He is not making any great protest against that; all he asks is that the government give him equal representation on the board which decides whether or not he is most essential to industry or to the armed forces. I do not think that is asking too much. The miners, the farmers, the steel workers and all other organized workers already have demonstrated in many ways that they are deeply concerned in winning the war. I do not think any group in Canada is more cognizant of the necessity of winning the war than the organized workers of this country; for they know something of nazism and what it stands for and what they may expect in the future if we lose. I submit therefore that arrangements should be made to have the officials of the unions sit in with the board. These call-ups will not be made so very often. A board does not have to sit continuously. If it is necessary to take 400 or a 1,000 men from a given industry, I do not think it is too much to ask that the organized workers sit in with that board and decide whether a man is more essential here, turning out aeroplanes, tanks or other equipment vital to the war effort, or whether he is more essential to the army. That is all they are asking. I leave that thought with the minister for his consideration.
Before this discussion is concluded I should be glad if the minister would give us some information as to the -latitude allowed in connection with national selective service. We have set up a national organization. From what I have gathered, that organization is in the hands of a very capable man. Has he sufficient latitude in administering the regulations, in connection with the particular
angle of calling men for military service? Has he the latitude to administer that organization as he sees fit, under the regulations, or is he subject to direction and control by national war services, agriculture, pensions and national health, and labour? The ramifications of these regulations reach into all these departments.
In addition I should like to ask the minister whether any consideration has been given to this aspect of the matter: Canada has not unlimited man-power. To a large extent she will be the arsenal of the British empire. Upon his recent visit to Canada General McNaughton stated that so far as Canada was concerned emphasis would have to be placed on war production. What proportion of the man-power of Canada is to be placed in the armed forces? After consultation with representatives of other allied nations has the government reached any understanding as to what is necessary for Canada by way of man-power, recognizing of course that at the same time, for the duration of the war, we shall have to maintain industrial production in Canada to an extent undreamed of in the past?

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Cape Breton South has raised questions of prime importance, which will require careful consideration not only by hon. members but by the people of Canada generally.
Before dealing specifically with the points raised by the hon. member toward the conclusion of his address, I should like to attempt to -clear up some misunderstanding which may be in his mind. If he will read the statement made by the Prime Minister on March 24 he will see that in the main the national selective service system is placed under the jurisdiction of the Department of Labour, but he will also see that the administration of the compulsory features of the national selective service system, in so far as it relates to the calling of men for military training, and subsequently for service in the army for the duration of the war, is in the Department of National War Services.
On a number of occasions I have pointed out the composition of the divisional boards, of which there are thirteen. Each board consists of three members, headed by a judge of a superior court or some other court of the province in which the major portion of the division is located. Then there are four persons who have the right to appear before and make representations to the board. They

War Appropriation-War Services
are not members of the board, but have the right to appear before it and make whatever representations they deem fit.
Who are these people?

One of them is a representative of the Department of National Defence. He is usually a serving officer of that department, and is assigned by it to that particular duty. The second representative is from the national war labour board, and is appointed by and representative of that body. The third representative is from agriculture. Then there is also the representative of the director of national selective service, who has the right to appear before and make representations to the board.
The idea behind the scheme is that the representatives of the Department of National Defence, the national war labour board and agriculture are present to see that the interests, if I may use that expression, of those chree groups, and the war objectives I mentioned some time ago, are safeguarded. I pointed out earlier that there were three war objectives, namely the raising of armed forces, the production of munitions of war and other war materials, and the supplying of food for shipment overseas. Let us look upon these as our three war objectives. These representatives when appearing before the board are, in a sense, guardians of those three objectives.
My point is that at present there is no one in authority to safeguard the production end of the matter.

Oh, yes; I do not think the hon. member and I are very far apart, in reality. For example, the purpose of having a representative from the national war labour board is to see that the needs of essential industry are safeguarded. It would be his duty to indicate to the board his opinion as to whether a man should be called for military training, or whether his call should be postponed on the ground of his being essential to war industry or being attached to some other necessary activities.
What is the function of the national selective service representative?

We recently added to the list of representatives the representative of the director of national selective service. He is there to see that so far as possible the best disposition of individual cases is made. So that in reality those persons with whom my hon. friend is chiefly concerned have two guardians, namely, the representative of the national war labour board and that of the director of national selective service.
Mr. MaeINNIS: That depends on who the representative of the national war labour board would be.

In all these matters the personal factor must enter; but the purpose of having these representatives appear before the board and make their representations to it is that of effecting a safeguard with respect to the various aspects and objectives of the war effort.
Do the boards consider these cases before the men are called, or do they function in the manner indicated after applications for postponements have been made?

The general practice is that the divisional registrar will send out a notice to report for medical examination. He will not know the position of any particular individual. If a man is rated category A-l, and does not make any application for postponement, the notice to report for military training at a certain training centre goes out to him in due course.

What opportunity
would he have of knowing in what category he was placed, if his own family physician did not tell him? Then, what opportunity would he have to ask for postponement?
When he gets the notice to report for medical examination, at the same time, through a memorandum of instructions he receives, he is advised as to his right to apply for postponement.
How would he know in what category he was?

I should like to reply to the hon. member for Cape Breton South, if I may. In a sense the board is really operating in respect of persons who have received notices to report for medical examination and have applied for the postponement of their military training-the board is operating a selective service system based upon the consideration of each individual case.
A man makes application for postponement, let us say on the ground that he is essential to war industry. The facts with regard to that man are on his card, but there may be other facts available. The representative of the Department of National Defence has a chance to make his representations. The representative of the national war labour board has the right to make his representations. There is also present a representative of the director of national selective service. Furthermore, the employer has a right to give evidence before the board as to the nature

War Appropriation-War Services
of the man's work, whether or not he can support the employee's application for postponement upon the ground that he is essential to war industry. The board attempts to ascertain whether the cpnsiderations are such that the man should go to military training, or whether his military training should be postponed. They consider each individual case from the point of view of all the facts. They hear whatever evidence is forthcoming with regard to the man's case. The various representatives make their representations. I think it may fairly be said that the board is operating a national selective service system when considering all the facts in a particular individual's case. After hearing the evidence in support of a man's application for postponement and the representations made on his behalf, the board makes its decision in the matter, which is final. In making this decision it is really operating a national selective service system on an individual basis.

Is it not true that the onus for the selective service rests upon the indivdual? Suppose a tool-maker were called up; whether he remains in industry or goes into the army will depend upon whether he asks for exemption.

Asks for postponement,
yes.

Whether a man stays in industry or goes into the army depends upon whether he asks for postponement. That is what governs, not that Mr. Little or anyone else makes the decision. The final decision rests with the man who is called.

In respect of the man who is quite willing to go into military training when he is called. The system does not entirely end there, because there is an arrangement with national defence under which a man may be brought out of the army under certain circumstances if he is considered a key man in war industry. Under the present system he cannot be brought out against his own will. We have not yet reached the point where a man can be pulled out of the army and put back into industry against his own will.
Can he be taken from one industry and placed in another against his own will?

We have not reached that stage either. I do not want to be guilty of the charge laid against me by the hon. member for Cape Breton South that I am answering for other departments. However, I think I have stuck to my own department to a
far greater extent than the hon. member for Cape Breton South has indicated. The boards try to arrive at a disposition of these cases according to certain principles, which are set out in the main in section 14 of the regulations. The board must consider certain classes of application from the point of view of the national interest and of all the surrounding circumstances. A study of the figures that have been given will indicate that the boards across Canada have looked with great care at these applications for postponement, and that the representatives of the various interests that I have mentioned have in the main done their duty and have safeguarded these various purposes in relation to the war effort.
Is there any uniformity in the decisions across the country? Is it not a fact that in some places they construe them quite narrowly while in others wide latitude is given?
The figures which I placed on Hansard some time ago indicate that there is a certain spread.
In Quebec it is very wide and in Saskatchewan it is quite low.
No, that is absolutely not right.
That is the deduction I make from the figures.

I am sure my hon. friend does not want to be unfair to any portion of Canada in connection with the granting of applications for postponement. The figures and percentages were placed on Hansard on May 11 and May 18.

I am trying to get this straight in my own mind because I am receiving a number of letters from people in western Canada. The minister said that the initiative in the application for postponement must come from the individual.
That is right.

Look at the Prime Minister's speech of March 24, at page 1566 of Hansard, where he said:
The liability to compulsory military service will continue to be general for the age categories affected. The burden of demonstrating the case for postponements is unchanged, except in the case of persons wholly or mainly employed in agriculture on March 23, 1942, as defined in the amended national war services regulations.

Will the hon. gentleman read the next sentence?

War Appropriation-War Services

He goes on:
One of the man-power problems with which the country is faced is the growing shortage of agricultural labour. Means, accordingly, have had to be devised to ensure that the supply of farm labour it not depleted. To that end, regulations have been enacted to stabilize employment in agriculture.
Keep on reading, please. The next sentence is the one.

He goes on:
With three exceptions, the regulations provide that no male person wholly or mainly employed in agriculture on March 23, 1942, as defined by the regulations shall enter into any employment outside agriculture unless he has obtained written permission from the national selective service officer to enter such employment. They also provide that no person shall take into employment outside agriculture, any male person wholly or mainly employed in agriculture unless such male person has obtained such permission.
Then a statement follows to the effect that persons wholly or mainly employed in agriculture will not normally be called up for military training.

I will read the next sentence:
The three exceptions provided for are active service in the armed forces by voluntary enlistment, seasonal employment in a primary industry, and compulsory military training if it is established that the person concerned is not an essential worker in agriculture.
But it has to be established that the man is not an essential worker in agriculture. That is the whole point. It is the interpretation of this speech and of the regulations in different parts of Canada that is causing all the difficulty.

My hon. friend has made a great deal out of that point of view. We have already covered in detail the application of the regulations relating to persons wholly or mainly employed in agriculture, on May 11 and again on May 18, and several times since then. I think it is perfectly clear, both from the Prime Minister's speech in the house and from my official press release of April 17, what the government's policy is. It was also fully dealt with by the conference of chairmen and registrars of the administrative divisions and I do not think I can usefully add anything to what has been already said.
With regard to the point of view put forward by the leader of the opposition, there is, I agree, a certain amount of apparent lack of uniformity in dealing with applications for postponement. Before one can conclude whether that apparent lack of uniformity is real or only apparent he must have possession of

all the facts and of the differences of situations in the various provinces. But that there is some variation is unquestioned; I do not see how you can get away from some variation when you have the personal factor and, what is more important than anything else, when you have each decision made upon the facts of that particular situation.
Let me now come to some of the specific points raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. He spoke of organized workers and their willingness to cooperate to the fullest extent in the war effort. I should like to pay my tribute to the manner in which workers in every part of Canada have answered the call when it was made to them.
The board must find the facts as to whether it is in the national interest that a man should receive postponement from military training if, for example, he is in a war industry. They must find that as a question of fact. They hear representations and take evidence. Furthermore all the boards, I think in all parts of Canada, where there are large centres or where there is a considerable concentration of war industry in their divisions, have visited those industries and know pretty well their whole set-up. In a number of the divisions at any rate the whole situation relating to war industry has been worked out. The board knows pretty well who are the essential indispensable key men, who are the highly skilled men and who are the semi-skilled men; they know who are the beginners and learners. This system of working out plans for dealing with war industry in the large centres has been highly satisfactory.
When my hon. friend says that the boards need not sit continuously, I may say to him that to deal with individuals in the way that I have indicated becomes increasingly difficult and takes an increasing amount of time as the number of persons who come before the boards for review grows.
The director of national service has not the deciding say in the matter of compulsory calling of men for military training and subsequent service in the Canadian army for the duration of the war. That is not a function of the director of national selective service. The director has a great many other functions, but this function is not one of them. It is a function that is performed by the Department of National War Services through the thirteen administrative boards I have mentioned and operating in the way I have indicated.
I agree with my hon. friend that Canada has not unlimited man-power, and it therefore becomes a matter of the utmost importance to utilize such man-power as exists in the best possible way and in such a manner as will

War Appropriation-War Services
make for the greatest effectiveness in the war effort of our country. It may be difficult at any one stage to say which of the three objectives I have mentioned is the most important at any one time. The Minister of National Defence has indicated what our objective in the matter of the armed forces is so far as man-power requirements are concerned. Roughly it is that we should have by the end of March, 1943, something over
600.000	enlisted men in our armed forces-that
is, in the army, in the air force and in the navy-he has given a breakdown of that. He indicated also what the strength of the armed forces was at the time he made that statement. Similarly, the Minister of Munitions and Supply indicated the man-power requirements for his programme:	that we have
600.000	persons engaged in war industry production, and that it was expected that another
100.000	would be employed therein by the end of March, 1943, and that a large part of the additional personnel would be women.
That is the programme which has been set, and it is believed that there is sufficient manpower to carry it out. That is the programme relating to the armed forces which was laid down by the Minister of National Defence, and the programme with regard to munitions production which was laid down by the Minister of Munitions and Supply, at the same time holding for agriculture the persons who are allocated to agriculture as a result of recent regulations relating to it. When we reach the objective of that particular programme we shall have to consider, of course, where we go from there. At this particular stage I do not see how it would be possible to indicate too far in advance what the respective objectives in the matter of man-power requirements should be. At the present time we are trying to attain all the objectives which I have mentioned as we have set them. In other words we are marching abreast towards the fulfilment of the programme which I have outlined. So far as the call-up for military training is concerned, in some divisions of Canada we are almost at the stage of exhaustion of the men in the age groups that we have called up thus far, and in other parts of Canada we are getting very close to that stage. As I indicated earlier, the reserves of man-power available for call for military training and subsequent service in the army vary in different parts of the country, as a result of many different causes.

Would the minister allow a question at this point? Apparently a survey has been made to ascertain how many men within the various age limits are still available for service. Is the minister in a
position to say that the point of exhaustion is being approached in certain military districts? Will he give the committee the figures showing the numbers in the different districts between ages 21 and 24 and 24 to 30 who are still available for war service?

That may not be so easy to do. I indicated at one stage that when we had the figures showing, for example, the impact of recent agricultural regulations on the man-power situation we would be in a better position to readjust the break-down of the requisitions that come from the Department of National Defence to the Department of National War Services.
They only ask you for so many men.
We will then be very close to the information which the hon. member for Lake Centre has in mind.

The information
must be available, on the basis of national registration, which will show exactly the number of young men in the various age classes and the records of the numbers who have been called up.
Oh, yes.

Then we would
necessarily have, by a simple subtraction, the numbers that are available, both medically fit and unfit.
I think I put on Hansard last November figures showing the numbers of men in each age group straight across Canada, by administrative divisions, and I think by provinces as well.
Then it is necessary to get enlistments, too, and calls.

If you deduct from that
the number of enlistments and the number of calls you would have still a great many deductions to make. You have the large deduction of persons who are below category A-l at the present time. I think I could name quite a number of deductions which would have to be made, in respect of persons who are engaged in essential occupations-war industry, agriculture and other occupations which are in the national interest.

Mr. Chairman,
there is only one way in which the minister can possibly say that the point of exhaustion is being arrived at, and that this committee may know just whether selective service is needed to-day, and that is to have the statistics of the pool of men who, if they would

War Appropriation-War Services
enlist, would be available for service. I cannot understand the answer of the minister this afternoon when he stated that, after the expiration of two months, the government is still not in a position to advise this committee and the country when the system of calling men by lot is to be brought into effect, and what the nature of the system will be.

Just before the minister
answers, I do not think the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) is fair to the minister. There is not a minister who has been more extensive in his remarks and in his answers-

That is another way of
putting it!

-than the Minister of National War Services. The hon. member for Lake Centre is asking for a tabulation. I wonder if he himself could recite a page of logarithms and give all sorts of figures of the kind. I know he understands my point, because he is a bright lawyer and an experienced debater, and he cannot expect the minister to give him off the bat such a number of figures. I am sure the minister will give him the information as soon as he has had time to tabulate it. Ministers may come here with their officials, but no one comes here with an adding machine and a typewriter to give information in this cafeteria for statistics. My hon. friend knows better than that.
If I am permitted I will tell the minister what my understanding is of the working of the department in getting men. It seems to me that the three defence departments, army, navy and air, are using the Department of National War Services for gathering men just the same as they apply to the Department of Munitions and Supply for munitions and supplies. The Department of National War Services, in that respect, is acting pretty much the same as the Department of Munitions and Supply and is helping the Department of National Defence. The requisitions for men come naturally through the Department of National Defence-from the three defence departments.
From one.

They come to the Department of National War Services. According to a news item that appeared not long ago, on May 16, in the press, draftees can now switch to the navy or the air force, but they must enlist either in the air force or in the navy before they are called by the Department of National War Services for training. It is a

new step towards disguised conscription, and I do not appreciate that method of dealing with trainees, because sometimes some of them have been waiting for a considerable period to get an answer from the board and they have to enlist at once either in the navy or in the air force, if they have inclinations towards those branches of the service, if they want to be accepted; otherwise they have not that choice any longer.
The change mentioned by the Prime Minister in his statement of March 24 indicated that the onus probandi, the weight of evidence, had been altered. First, it was the draftee, the trainee or the conscript who had to prove that his training should be delayed for one reason or another, and then it was up to the board to decide whether the evidence was enough to justify such a delay. Now when a trainee states that he is indispensable to the farm and asks for a delay it is the duty of the board or of someone else connected with the board to show that such is not the case, that the man is not indispensable to the farm.
The law is the other way. The young man who applies must prove his case.

I am coming to that. All that was required according to the regulations was that the draftee when he was called had to undergo his medical examination, something he always had to do, and then write to the registrar informing him of the reasons why it was impossible for him to go. That was the former practice. But now, although it is said that the statement of the draftee that he is indispensable to farming is prima facie evidence, and although that has been broadcast in the press, the practice is altogether different from that indicated in the statements that have been given to the press. The young man has to give a sworn statement to the effect that he is a bona fide farmer, that his presence on the farm is indispensable, and then the board does not require contrary evidence to refuse his request. But the board takes upon itself to accept or reject such evidence, which seems contrary to the statement made by the Prime Minister, and contrary to what the Minister of National War Services has just said.
If we take the request of the young men in the army who have to get leave to help their parents on the farm, the procedure is much more complicated. There must be a sworn request giving all data and sworn to by the draftee himself; and in the second place there must be two other sworn statements of persons who are not related to him. How can it be said afterwards that the weight of

War Appropriation-War Services
evidence has been transferred from the private individual to the state when the private individual is required to bring forth so much, and especially when the board many times pays no attention to that evidence and decides just the same as if there were weightier contrary evidence when there is none? Take the case of a particular farmer. Let us call him A. He is a young man whose father and mother are dead and he is the only support of his younger brothers and sisters. The condition of his health is not very good and he earns enough money in civil life to provide support for the whole family. That young man is in the position of a married man with a family, and if he brings his case, supported by the mayor and by the parish priest and proves that it is a cruel hardship, the board can come to this decision: No; we will pay no attention to that evidence; go to your training. And then if a young man who is already in the army submits his request to his commanding officer, the commanding officer is supposed to transmit that request to the board. But it is optional with him. He can refuse. He may grant certain leave, but on the other hand he may say, "No, I will simply keep that request on my desk".
I have here the case of a young man, E-615935, a soldier at Valcartier, who on April 27 submitted his request for leave to his commanding officer and up to May 27 had heard nothing about it. It is very embarrassing to leave people under a false impression. Of course I believe that everything that has been said about it has been said in good faith; but when boys who were on the farms saw in the press that on March 23 all those who were then on the farm were frozen on the farm, they said: "What is the use of reporting? We are already exempt; at last we have that exemption that we had during the last war." Moreover, the newspapers gave a good deal of publicity to the matter and those boys who were in good faith found to their surprise afterwards that they were deserters because they stayed on the farm and worked there on the very day when all those who were doing so were supposed to be exempt. I want hon. members to understand the situation.
Nobody can understand it.

I am trying to explain what happened, and I admit it is a cobweb. But what I want hon. members to understand is that these young men are acting in good faith and they have been deceived by statements made in good faith. But not only
that. The situation looks complicated, but it is really much worse. There is a distinction between those who had one month of training and those who had four months. It is a subtle distinction that must have originated in the mind of that eminent counsel who before the war was lobbyist de luxe for John de Iiuyper's concoction.
You don't like John de Kuyper?
It is not that, but I do not see how anyone can describe as eminent counsel one who was a lobbyist de luxe for John de Kuyper's concoction.
Who was he?

That will come out in due course. Here is the case of E-615608. I have a sworn statement which I will summarize. It is the case of a young farmer. He said that on December 22 he was on temporary leave and visited his family and did not return to the camp and they told him he was a deserter. He stayed with his father to help him with his work on the farm. The father needed him. He said his father's farm consisted of 200 acres, of which 135 were cultivated, and that on the farm there were five horses, twelve cows, four calves, twelve hogs; sheep, hens and chickens. He was the only son who could help his father in the work. That was why he could not return to the camp. This letter is dated May 2, but this young man was on the farm on March 23 and notwithstanding that, he is supposed to be a deserter.
Here is the case of F-13800, another farmer's son, whose father is very ill. There is a certificate from the hospital stating that the father has been in hospital and that he cannot work on the farm. The farm is a large one. There is a certificate from the mayor who is also warden of the county, and it is impossible for that young man to get an answer from the board.
Here is another case, that of a son of a baker who was sick and could not work. This is the case of F-67322. The father could not work and was replaced by his eldest son who did the work in the bakery. The boy went to his training and was replaced by his younger brother. The younger brother is needed at home because he is the support of the family during his father's illness. The case has been submitted to the board but there has been no answer yet.
I have received very many letters. I will only read two that have come to me, one from the county of Bona venture and the other

War Appropriation-War Services
from St. Valerien, Rimouski county. I will send a copy to the minister. He is a linguist and knows both languages very well. I quote:
(Translation.)
St-Charles Caplan, May 28, 1942.
Sir,
Although I am not a resident of your constituency, I beg leave to submit my case to you. I am a farmer and the only son I have who might be of assistance to me is undergoing military training. I have tried in vain to have him released for the summer in order that I might have the help I need on my farms, and the steps I have taken are as follows.
I wrote to Mr. Henri Paul Drouin (reg.), and to Capt. Laniel, of Rimouski. I was referred to Colonel Chaloult, of Quebec. My son was sent to Three Rivers; I wrote to Colonel Forbes, forwarding under the same cover a letter from the parish priest, signed by the mayor, asking that an investigation be made on the spot, if necessary, following which I mailed two other communications. You may appreciate success of my endeavours when I tell you that all I have received, since March 31 last, was a reply stating that my request had been referred to the Department of National Defence.
I own three farms, three hundred chickens, one hundred hens, twenty-three head of cattle, four horses, one tractor and twelve hogs. I have a family of seventeen children to look after, the eldest of whom are girls. My only helpers are a cripple who spent five years in a hospital and is unable to work hard, and a grandson of thirteen who still attends Sunday school. You will easily see that I cannot get along without additional assistance. Although I do my best, I must 'perforce neglect a great many things. _ The authorities encourage agricultural production and at the same time deprive me of the only valuable assistance I had. Is this fair? I am already exhausted, and the -work is far from done. I hope, Mr. Member, that you will not remain indifferent to my appeal, for otherwise I do not know to whom I should turn in order to obtain a modicum of justice.
You may be sure that I shall be very grateful for anything you do on my behalf.
Yours faithfully,
That is one. The other one is from Rimouski, and is as follows:
St-Valerien, May 27, 1942.
Dear Sir,
You may find it strange to receive a letter from a resident of another constituency, especially on this subject, but a friend in Rimouski advised me to write to you.
Here is my problem: I have a son who entered the army on Dec. 4; he is a farmer's son and we absolutely need him on the land. I requested that he be allowed to return home during seed-time and to help me build a barn. However, no leave was granted to him. I have lost the only helper I could really count on, and I have six acres of land by forty in length. . . .
He says his farm is one of 240 acres. It continues:
... I have a youngster with me, but he is not accustomed to handling farm machinery.
My son underwent two months' training in Three Rivers and Rimouski, was then sent to
fMr. Pouliot.]
Sherbrooke and from there to Sussex, N.B. He again applied for leave in Sussex, and they seem to be taking this under consideration. If you were able to assist us in the matter, I think we could succeed. We did not object to his undergoing four months' training, but we would like to have had him on the farm at seed-time and until after the harvest. It is too bad to see him penned in down there when he loves the land so much. During his three days' leave, he took time out to plough a field.
In conclusion, I trust that you will be able to help us. I shall need his services badly when I start to build my barn in June.
(Text) This is another case with respect to a young man, a farmer, who took advantage of his three days of leave to do some ploughing.
Did he overstay ?

No; he went back to his regiment. We complain of the shortness of the delay in making the call; the young men have no time to present their cases to the board. I have in mind the case of F-21457. This was a young man who had been sick at home, and who was notified that if he did not go at once for his medical examination the mounted police would be sent after him. This happened during the winter when there were enormous snowbanks on the ground, and it was very cold. This young man had to leave his bed to go for medical examination.
This sort of thing has happened not only in Quebec; the same has happened at Cornwall. A returned man, who is working in the House of Commons, came to me to complain about the way in which his son had been treated at Cornwall. The boy had been home, and while home had developed pleurisy. However, the military authorities wanted him at once in Cornwall, and they brought him back in a truck.
Who did?
The army military police. Then I have in mind another case with respect to a young man who was placed in category A.
How many cases has the hon. member?

If my hon. friend has some cases in his constituency, he will be free to bring them to the attention of the committee. If he is not interested, he may go back behind the curtain and smoke a cigarette. I am working for my electors, and no power will prevent me from defending them. Besides that, I am not affected by jeers or ridicule; they leave me entirely indifferent. If my hon. friend wants to know how many cases I have, he has only to listen to me and count on his fingers, to save time. I do not wish to be offensive; I

War Appropriation-War Services
like the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare; he is a friend of mine, but I will not stand for any interruptions when I am defending the case of a farmer in this country.
And the hon. member is making a good job of it.

I do not know whether it is good or bad, but I do my duty to the best of my ability. I am sorry I have not the eloquence of some hon. members. This is not funny work; my files are open to all, and it will be seen that I look after my people. Moreover, I have an office at Riviere du Loup just to look after farmers' sons; that is the only work my secretary is doing there. There is also the tremendous amount of correspondence I have here. I attend to that seriously; it is not a joke. Anyone can call me this or that; I do not care. But when it comes to the defence of my electors, I am behind them, because I know they stand by me when I need them.
Not only have I cases from my constituency; I have some from Ottawa. For instance, here is the case of Mr. James O'Meara, of 67 Red-path street, Ottawa, who speaks for his son. This is a general complaint about the way in which things are being done. I do not blame the minister, but I wish him to understand what is happening. I am willing to cooperate with him, and I am also ready to help him redress the wrong. Wrongs must be redressed.
If we must have conscription, then let us see that we have conscription, and we shall know where we stand. But when we are hearing about a voluntary system, and people having no opportunity to defend themselves, I find it unjust and unfair. That is why I fight for my people. I believe we have a voluntary system, and I believe in the law; this is a matter of law. But if we are to have conscription, then let us say, "there is conscription for overseas. We do not want to bother about the defence of this country. We are thinking about the defence of other lands." If we hear that, then we shall know where we stand' and what to say. But as long as we have the so-called voluntary system, and as long as the voluntary system is not working well, it is the duty of each member of parliament to defend his electors. He should explain the cases having to do with farmers. We are not yet eating soya beans, but I hear that experiments have been made. If soya beans are used, the farmers will be even more useful. We need the farmers; they are essential and vital to our war effort. They are just as vital as the soldiers, because if there were no farmers the soldiers would not be fed.

This is to certify that Harold O'Meara was a patient in the Ottawa General hospital from April 17, to August 6, 1933. He was treated for a traumatic cataract.

Your letter of March 14, 1942, addressed to Captain Williams, R.C.O.C., Lansdowne park, has been passed to this H.Q. for attention.
Upon investigating this case it has been found that a Harold O'Meara, giving his address of 67 Redpath street, presented himself for enlistment in the first Canadian ordnance field park, Ii.C.O.C., and was medically categorized E for high blood pressure.
