It is quite extraordinary to read in this letter that the Department of National Defence must ask a father to give evidence as to whether his son is sick. The next letter has reference to the information received from England. In England they came to an entirely different conclusion. This man was first placed in category E; then a month later he was placed in category A and later in England he was placed in another category. The letter reads:
Cable advice has been received to the effect that your son, Pte. H. W. O'Meara, C38005, has been medically boarded in England and placed in category Cl.
Ordinarily category Cl means that a soldier is fit for service in Canada only. However, permission has been granted to retain category Cl men in England if their services are required there.
I am unable, therefore, to advise you as to whether or not your son will be returned to Canada because he has been lowered in category.
That is just one case. There is no excuse for such things happening. We should try to
have a reform. There are some fellow members who are medical practitioners, such as
[Mr. Pouliot.l
the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Fleming) and the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) who is the dean of his profession, and I think they will agree with me that these medical examinations should be carried out with greater care. When the older Mr. O'Meara wrote to the Department of National Defence he was sent from pillar to post, and his son had to cross the Atlantic in order to get a grading more in conformity with the facts. Is this not absurd? I ask my colleagues to help me in getting this reform. It will be for the good of all. It is a bad thing when a man who is not medically fit is taken into the army just to satisfy the pride of the officer in charge of enlistments.
I realize that the minister is busy; I know he has one of the most ungrateful tasks in the whole government. He can rely upon me to help him, but we should not try to help him by agreeing with everything that is done. It is up to us to point out the bad spots so that he can use all the means at his disposal to bring about reform for the improvement of his department and the improvement of the army. I have many other cases to which I could refer. We cannot discuss these matters theoretically; we must bring up concrete cases.
The O'Meara case is a scandal, and I have other similar cases which occurred in my constituency. However, there has been an improvement in my district simply because I have fought hard over certain cases. I do not want to have to take charge of Kingston district, but when a man comes in and shows me correspondence like that it is my duty to place it on Hansard. I do not wish to have much to do with the Minister of National Defence because he is like Fabius, who used to temporize. It takes just as long to get an answer from the minister as it does to get results from squeezing a stone. If the Minister of National Defence cannot understand the arguments put forward by members of parliament, his colleagues may. It is with that hope that I make this argument. I expect to have some support, even inside the cabinet, in the reform of the wrongdoings in the Department of National Defence.
We see what is going on, and we want to improve the welfare of the soldier. We want to see that his sons and daughters are kept healthy. We want our soldiers to be well looked after and receive the proper treatment, not only when they are undergoing medical examination but when they are on sick parade. I know my hon. friends who are medical practitioners will be scandalized when I tell them that at the citadel at Quebec a soldier appeared on sick parade. The captain, the so-called doctor, asked him, "What is the matter with

War Appropriation-War Services
you?" He said, "I have a rupture." Do hon. members know what the answer of that doctor was? He said, "Get a good rub for the rupture." The man who was to give the rub was a lumberjack, with hands just as long as poles and as rough as sandpaper. He was to give a rubbing for a rupture. My medical Colleague, the hon. member for Humboldt smiles, but it is true. I have the actual file. Sometimes men who have been declared physically fit and classed in category A have come to my office and I have started my medical examination. AVithout pursuing it too far, I discovered that one man was suffering from a rupture-he was rejected and put in category E-another man had chronic appendicitis, and there was also a case of goitre.
I just asked them questions, and I found that the fault was just as much the local doctor's as the army doctor's. All of the doctors seem to want to send men, whether fit or not, into the army. The more the better seems to be their policy, without taking into consideration the actual state of health of the man. All these practices must stop.
Now that I have had my turn I will give way so that other hon. members may bring before the committee all their complaints.

There are three suggestions I should like to bring before the minister, each one of them having to do with the mobilization division of his Department of National AVar Services. That division, by the way, is a very important division and becoming more important every month as more and more men are called up for service.
My first suggestion has to do with the groups of young Canadians who are to be called up for military training and the order in which they are to be called. Last Thursday the minister made an announcement which was of the greatest importance, even though the announcement came out in the wash, so to speak, in the midst of questioning. It will be found at page 2872 of Hansard, where the minister is reported to have said:
But when we move the age group up-
Mr. Cruickshank: If.
Mr. Thorson: Not if, when. AVe will probably move up the age group very soon. AVe are now calling the age group of from twenty-one to thirty years, and I would not be at all surprised if we moved that forward to thirty-five years within a very short time.
I repeat, that was a very important announcement. For me it signified that there is uncertainty in the ministry as to the order in which these young Canadians are to be called up. There is also great uncertainty in this house; not one of us here can tell his constituents what men are to be called up next.
There is also uncertainty in the press. The result of the minister's announcement on Thursday night was that the press published such headlines as this, in the Montreal Star of Friday, May 30:
Pool of single men for draft running low. Extension of plans to 1907 class leads to married men.
From the Ottawa Journal of the same date I read this heading:
Married men may be called to the army. Start with those who were twenty-one in July, 1940.
The first paragraph of the article, which I think appeared in most of the large Canadian dailies, reads thus:
AVith mobilization authorities apparently scraping near the bottom of the pool of available single men of prime military age, the time draws nearer when married men may be called up for compulsory military service.
The result will be that there will be even greater uncertainty in the minds of the Canadian people. Let the minister picture the position of the men who may be called up to serve: for example, single men and widowers without children in the age group from thirty-one to thirty-five, the same classes of men in the age group from thirty-six to forty-five, the single men of nineteen and twenty, and the younger married men. All of these Canadians are wondering when they are to be called or whether they are to be called or not, and there is the greatest confusion.
It seems to me that the lack of a clear-cut policy is neither sound nor fair. Oui people are entitled to know, and to know well in advance, what groups are to be called up next. Indeed they are entitled to know in what order the groups are to be called, so that men can adjust their lives accordingly; and not only that the men can adjust their lives, but that their families and the firms foi which they work and other people with whom they are connected can also make the necessary arrangements. There is at present too much mystery about the whole matter. The ministry should decide without delay upon a policy as to the groups to be called next, the order in which they are to be called, and approximately when these groups will be called for service. Not only should they decide upon such a policy, but they should most carefully explain it to the Canadian people. It affects the lives of hundreds of thousands of Canadians, and there will be no success in the working out of the policy unless it is most carefully explained to our people. That is my first suggestion.

War Appropriation-War Services
The second is that the selection of men by lot from the groups called should be started now, without further delay. The switchover to this lottery system seems to be bound up tightly in red tape. Some of us advocated selection by lot many, many months ago. That system has been used in the United States from the start, where even before the war they called up men in the age group from twenty-one to thirty-five-I think those were the ages-by lot. This selection by lot is admittedly the fairer way. The minister himself said so. I quote his remarks at page 2312 of Hansard:
. . . we intend to change that method of calling men, and to make the call applicable to all the men in all the age groups covered by the proclamation. That is to be done by a system of drawing by lot. Back of that is the view-
Here are the important words:
Back of that is the view that that would be a more equitable manner of making the call. At present all men up to thirty years of age are covered by the proclamation, and are liable to call. It is now proposed to call these men by lot, and all the men in all the age groups subject to the proclamation will take their chances in the draw.
That was promised over two months ago by the Prime Minister, when he spoke in this house on March 24, and said, as reported at page 1566 of Hansard:
It has also been decided to select the men to be called up for service by drawing lots over the whole field of those who are subject to the proclamation.
When the minister himself spoke on May 11 he said that as soon as they could work out the administrative difficulties the call-up would be by lot, but as yet the government is selecting these men by juniority, as the minister said the other night. I think he was inventing a word, but it described the process very well, which is that the system so far has been to take the youngest age group and to go through that group before going into the next one.
The picture, as I understand it, is this. First of all, practically all of our men from twenty-two to twenty-six inclusive have already been taken in previous calls.

Not in all parts of
Canada.
The great majority of men of these ages have been taken, have they not?
It varies in different parts of Canada.

The call on March 24 was for those who would be twenty-one this year and for men who would be twenty-seven,

twenty-eight, twenty-nine and thirty during the present year. The minister on November 12 last placed on Hansard, page 4303, the figures of the single men in Canada as found by the national registration. I will not give the figures of each of these age groups that are now subject to call, but they total 291,838. Of that number, almost one-half, it is to be assumed, are unfit, so that approximately
150.000	men would be available. There have, however, been thousands upon thousands of enlistments from these groups, and if I am informed correctly the government has no accurate record of how many from these or any other groups have enlisted since national registration.
They must have.

No; they have no accurate record of the number who have enlisted. For example, we find in this morning's Ottawa Citizen a dispatch from Brockville district:
District man overseas receives his call-up.
Although he has been overseas for almost a year, Mrs. Maurice Grigsby, Hubbell street, received a registered letter from national defence headquarters, for her husband, Lieutenant M. G. Grigsby, notifying him of his call-up for a medical examination previous to entering a basic training centre for compulsory military training. Lieutenant Grigsby, who enlisted here more than a year ago, and who was the first Brockville boy to graduate from the officers' training centre, is with the R.C.A.S.C. He was recently made adjutant of his unit overseas.
Another case, which came to my attention two weeks ago, was that of a lad from Vancouver who received a call for service while home on his embarkation leave-having been in the army for nearly two years and won his commission.
Some of them are dead.

So I repeat that the government has no accurate record of how many young men have enlisted; to that extent it is working in the dark. Then, the figure of
150.000	would be further reduced by the numbers of farmers, farm labourers, and others who are exempted-for example, men in war industry. We have this picture, that the groups which were called on March 24 are now used up in some of the districts and nearly used up in others, so that there is little chance of many of these men being selected by lot. For them a call-up by lot is a farce; it is, I repeat, a farce as far as these men are concerned. In the group to which the minister referred the other night, single men and widowers from thirty-one to thirty-five inclusive, without children, there will be probably

War Appropriation-War Services
much the same situation. They, according to the national registration, numbered 140,944, and from that one would have to deduct about half as unfit.
More than that.
They are older men, and the percentage of unfit will accordingly be larger. Many of them, too, have enlisted. So that there is not a great number of men in that group. "
No.

I repeat that there should be no delay in beginning this selection by lot. Let the administrative staff shear through the red tape and get this new system started.
The third suggestion is that there should be no further delay in extending the liability for military service to all residents of Canada, whether citizens or not. The Prime Minister said on March 24, as reported in Hansard at page 1566:
Liability for compulsory military service is, at present, confined to citizens of Canada. It has been decided to extend this liability to all residents of Canada, whether citizens or not, as far as may be expedient in the light of all the circumstances.
Yet none of these non-citizens have been called up. When will they be called? This house and the Canadian people are entitled to know. I would remind the Minister of National War Services of his speech the other evening on equality of sacrifice, a speech which I thought was excellent. Yet here we have this situation: thousands and thousands of Canadian citizens have been called up, and in thousands of these cases their jobs have been taken over by young men of the same age who are not Canadian citizens and, in some instances, are enemy aliens but not interned. The Canadian people cannot be convinced that there is equality of sacrifice as long as that condition continues. It is unfair and dangerous that there should be such a long delay in calling up these non-citizens. I suggest that young men who are citizens of countries which are allies or are neutral should be called just as though they were Canadian citizens and should be put into the forces, and that enemy aliens who are not interned should be called for labour work; let them be put in a civilian construction corps. The government announced some months ago that that was to be done with some of the men of Japanese origin, but as far as I know the plan has never been worked out. I warn the government that this condition must be remedied.
We must not leave these non-citizens free to take the jobs of young Canadians who are being called up.
Those are the suggestions which I have for the minister. May I add something which, to a degree, is in his defence. I think one reason for the lack of a clear-cut policy on the calling up of men, for the delay in calling up by lot and for the delay in calling non-citizens is that, while the responsibility for getting men remains with the Department of National War Services, the power has been shifted to the Department of Labour.
No, no.

On March 24, selective service plans were announced. The orders in council then filed included one which transferred national registration, the records thereof and everything having to do with that registration to the Department of Labour. Therefore, when the Department of National War Services wants to call men, it must go to the Department of Labour, if you please, to get information.
Not at all. We have all the cards for the single men up to forty-five in the divisions.
Well, if the minister's department wants to get further information on any men, it must go to the Department of Labour.
No; we have all the cards relating to all men up to forty-five in the divisions.

I am trying to help the minister out, and he would be wise to keep still and let me fight his case for him. Another handicap is that under the same orders in council the director of national selective service has been put under the Deparment of Labour, not under the Department of National War Services. In other words, the emphasis has been placed on men for war industries rather than on men for the armed forces, and the result has been and will be confusion, and fewer men for the services. The Department of National War Services should have the last word on all those men in the age groups that have been called or are eventually to be called. This department is of vital importance, and, as I said in the beginning, is becoming more and more important all the time as more men are called. It can do more than any other department to bring about equality of sacrifice in the war effort and to keep high the morale of the Canadian people. But neither of these great

War Appropriation-War Services
objectives will be reached if there are indecision and delay-which exist at the present time unfortunately-in connection with phases of the work of the department such as the three that I have mentioned: what groups are to be called and in what order; selection by lot; and the calling up of non-citizens.

The hon. member for
Vancouver South (Mr. Green) has raised a number of questions which are really related to certain questions which the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) put a little earlier. I have been waiting for the first opportunity to deal with some of the questions put by the hon. member for Lake Centre. The question of how many men are available for military training and subsequent service in the army for the duration of the war is not an easy one to determine, for this reason. We know how many persons have received notices to report for medical examination. Those go out in the ordinary course. Then we know the number of men who have been rejected as being below category Al; and as we go into the higher age groups and deal with persons whose physical condition is not as good as the condition of those of earlier years, we run into an increasingly high percentage of persons who are found not medically fit for service in the armed forces. Then we have postponements on various grounds that have been mentioned. These postponements, in the opinion of the boards, at any rate, are made on the ground of national interest. If they are made on that basis and there are no more persons in the divisions to whom to send notices, except of course that there is always the continuing number of persons who become twenty-one, we can say-it is only relative, I will admit-that we have reached the point of exhaustion of our man-power reserve if we continue the men postponed in occupations which thus far have been deemed to be essential. That man-power pool or reserve for the purposes of the armed forces can be enlarged in these cases-
In the future.

but only if we strip
war industry or agriculture or other essential occupations of their man-power requirements. Whether it would be wise to do that depends upon the state of affairs at any one time; it depends upon the importance of any particular aspect or objective of the war effort at any one time. That, I think, was stressed by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), who expressed great concern for the steel workers in connection with the war effort. At one stage of the war it may be

absolutely essential to the successful prosecution of our effort that men should not be +aken out of war industry; yet who can tell what situation may develop, depending upon emergencies? It is hard to say, therefore, just what is the absolute limit of our man-power reserve, and I do not think we can make a purely statistical approach to the question of man-power reserve by reason of the many deductions that have to be made from statistical figures.

But does
that not depend upon the objective-the number of men that the government proposes to have in the army, and the number of reinforcements that are necessary to keep them going (a) in war time and (b), which is much more important, during the time when casualties begin to roll in?
Quite so.
And does it not depend upon how hard it is to beat the Germans and the Japs?

Of course, that is the
important thing, and it may be that manpower for purposes of the armed forces may be the most imperative need above all other needs. All I suggest is that we cannot be arbitrary in stating the priorities at any one time. I think the programme of our armed forces is based on an increase in the capital strength of the armed forces, and it is also based, as I understood the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), on two reserves of reinforcements. The one is the usual wastage reserve, which is fairly well known, month by month, and the other is the battle casualty reserve, which of course is a matter of estimate. There were a number of other points raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South, but it is now six o'clock.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

I was about to deal with some of the matters raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South. I appreciate what he said about the uncertainty in the minds of many men in this country as to the time when they will be called for military training and service for the duration of the war. But while I appreciate that uncertainty, I should also say that if we are to make the utmost use of our man-power reserve, and if we are to march toward the attainment of

War Appropriation-War Services
our various war objectives concurrently, we cannot avoid the feeling of uncertainty to which my hon. friend made reference; for war itself is a matter of uncertainty.
But why could the government not say which groups are to be called next; in other words, give the order of the groups?

Thus far we have been calling men by age groups, dealing with the lowest age group first, then marching into the next age group above that, and so on. I think it well when we reach, or come close to, the exhaustion of a set of age groups subject to proclamation, that we should indicate that fact in plenty of time, so that young men may be able to put their affairs in order. I think it is fairer to young men to make the announcement some time in advance of the time when they will be subject to call.
I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South in his expression of hope that the system of selecting men by lot may be put into effect as soon as possible. I think it is a fairer system than that in force at present, of exhausting a complete age group before going into a subsequent group. I think the system of selection by lot is very much fairer. Then everybody takes his chance by the lot. I can assure my hon. friend that the administrative matters which must be attended to before that system can be put into effect take some time to complete.
When will the lot system be put into effect?

I would not like to say. I should like to see the system in operation for the July call; but whether or not the administrative details can be worked out in order to make the system applicable to the July call, I cannot say at the moment. I can only assure my hon. friend that the matter is being worked on intensively.
My hon. friend made reference to one other matter, namely that notices to report for medical examination are sometimes sent out to persons who have already enlisted. In some instances that is absolutely inevitable, because the man who has enlisted does not notify anyone of his enlistment. He may enlist in one part of Canada while the address on his registration card is in another part of Canada, and it takes some time for those facts to reach the various registration divisions.
Does the Department of National Defence not notify the Department of National War Services?

The Department of
National Defence does its best to keep the Department of National War Services continuously informed as to enlistments.
How long have they been doing that?
Oh, for some time. The situation is better now than it was previously.
They did not originally, did they?
Well, they were not too good about it. But that situation is improving, though of course that notification is not instantaneous. It cannot be, by its very nature.
It seems to take a couple of years in some instances.

Well, I would not go so far as to say that, and I am sure my hon. friend does not mean it either. Then, too, there may be a number of other reasons why notices may be sent to persons who are no longer available. They may have moved; perhaps in some instances they have died. Sometimes that likewise is quite inevitable; but we are endeavouring as far as possible to eliminate all those persons to whom notices to report for medical examination should not be sent. That takes a little time. Then the cards have to be dealt with, and there are many thousands of them. My hon. friend quoted from a return the number of single men in the age groups from twenty-one to forty-five. They extend into the hundreds of thousands. I assure my hon. friend that it is not an easy matter to work into this system, which I think is fairer than the present one; but we are making as much headway as possible with the administrative arrangements, and just as soon as the administrative details have been worked out I shall make the announcement to which the Prime Minister referred.
The third suggestion which my hon. friend made is that all residents of Canada, whatever their citizenship may be, should as far as possible be made subject to the national war services regulations.
I did not advocate that enemy aliens should be called for military service.
Of course there would be some qualification in the matter of enemy aliens.
I recommended that they be put on labouring work.

Yes; but even enemy aliens, while not made subject to the national war service regulations, from the point of view

War Appropriation-War Services
of their being included in the armed forces, might become subject to the regulations for some kind of alternative service, just as we make the Mennonites, Doukhobors and conscientious objectors, whose cases. are postponed as far as their military training is concerned, subject to alternative service.
The Prime Minister made the announcement that it was the policy of the government to make all residents of Canada subject to the regulations. The matter of policy is settled, but there are arrangements to be made in connection with the various classes and categories of aliens. There are a number of categories of aliens which would have to be considered in the matter. There are those who are citizens of allied countries. They can be dealt with by an interchange of regulations. We have gone a very great distance in that respect, as far as our relations with the United States are concerned. Then there are the aliens who are citizens of neutral countries. They are in a somewhat different category, but arrangements can be and are being worked out with regard to them.
When will they be subject to call?

The amendments relating to aliens will be announced in the near future.
I do not believe I can go any further than that.
Have they been drafted?
There have been several drafts.
They are amendments to what?

Amendments to the
national war services regulations, making the regulations applicable to persons resident in Canada, regardless of their nationality.
Does the minister mean that the aliens have been drafted, or the regulations?

The regulations are being drafted. Then, there are the citizens of enemy alien countries. Further, there are various aliens who are stateless persons. In addition, there are British subjects who are nationals of the various British dominions, and who are not ordinarily resident in Canada, but are here for the time being.
Are they subject to call?

Not as yet, under the regulations as they stand to-day. The present regulations are applicable only to every male 
British subject who is or who has been at any time subsequent to September 1, 1939, ordinarily resident in Canada.
The dominion has given authority to certain of our allies to recruit their nationals in Canada. That authority has been given with respect to Netherlanders, Belgians, Norwegians, Poles and Czechs; but we have not yet given any of our allies the power to conscript their own nationals.
It is all on a voluntary basis?
Yes. We have worked out certain draft conventions with the United States relating to draft evaders and deserters.
I notice we are opening recruiting offices in the United States. Can the minister tell us anything about that?

No; I know no more about that than the leader of the opposition has seen in the press. The matter of working out the necessary amendments to the regulations is intricate, but in some instances reciprocal arrangements are being worked out. In others it is desirable to communicate with representatives of the countries involved, so that they will deal with our nationals in the same way as we deal with theirs, and not otherwise.
The number of aliens in Canada is surprisingly small. Last fall I placed on Hansard a table showing the number of aliens in Canada, and I was very much surprised by the smallness of the number.
That ought to make it all the easier to get action in the matter.

Yes, it makes it easier. I do not anticipate any real difficulty at all, when we have worked out the necessary amendments. When those amendments have been decided upon they will be enacted, and then residents of Canada who are not now subject to the regulations will become subject to them, and called up in due course.
Will they cover young enemy aliens also?

I think we could work out regulations dealing with enemy aliens, just as we are working on a number of other amendments to the regulations for the purpose of using certain persons who are below category A-l, and therefore not fit for those services in the armed forces which require men of a high category, for other purposes. We may be able to use such men for some other activity that may be in the national interest. The regulations are capable of expansion in a variety

War Appropriation-War Services
of ways. I have no doubt that we can work out regulations that will deal satisfactorily with enemy aliens.

After single men and
widowers without children between the ages of twenty-one and thirty-five years have been called, what age groups will then be called?

I do not think I can make any statement at this stage with regard to that. As I pointed out a moment ago, the regulations are applicable to "every male British subject who is or who has been at any time subsequent to the first day of September, 1939, ordinarily resident in Canada, while he is of the ages of twenty-one years to forty-five years inclusive and who was on the fifteenth day of July, 1940, unmarried or a widower without child or children." The regulations apply to such persons, but the only persons who are subject to call are those in the age groups specified in the proclamation issued pursuant to these regulations.
Where a man enlists in the air force for air crew, and becomes washed up and is discharged, will he be liable to call for training in the army?

Technically he is subject to call. Under section 13, I think it is, we can recall such men. I am not sure that we have not done so in some instances. A person may be rejected for certain reasons by the air force and still be perfectly fit according to army standards. He may fail in some quality essential to air force standards but have all the qualities required by army standards.

I have been told that in some districts this is rather prevalent. It is quite easy to become washed up and discharged, but I understand that in some places they are not then being called up for the army.
They may get notice to report for medical examination under our regulations.

Are there many cases where the physician making the preliminary examination passes a man, and then later on he is reexamined and put in category E as permanently unfit? A man is permitted to visit his family physician for examination, but he is not told in what category he is placed. He receives his call, send perhaps after a week or so of training he is examined by the medical authorities and found to be in category E.

There have been cases where not only the original physician but the medical revision board have marked a man as category Al, and then after he has
reported to the training centre and has submitted himself for examination by an army medical board, he is rejected. The full extent of these rejections can be seen from the tables I placed on Hansard. One table shows the number of persons requisitioned by the Department of National Defence. Another table shows the number of men who have been ordered to report to training centres. All these men would be graded category A. Then a third table shows the number of persons actually accepted at the training centres as being fit. A comparison of the third and second tables will show the percentage of rejections by army medical boards of men who have been passed category A either by the doctor of their choice in the first instance or by our revision boards.

What time elapses between a man going to his own physician for a preliminary examination and the time he is told to report? There was brought to my attention last week the case of a man who received a notice to report. On Friday this man had his examination, but not knowing in what category he was placed he did not make an application for postponement on the ground of being engaged in an essential war industry, that is, an aircraft plant. On a week from the following Monday he received a notice to report at the Connaught ranges in Ottawa. The notice was received on Monday evening at 6.30 o'clock, and he was to report on Thursday morning. He had no opportunity to place his case before a board because the time between the receipt of his first notice to report to a doctor and the time he was supposed to report for training was only eight days. Is that the usual length of time granted these people?

As I pointed out this
afternoon, a man receives two documents, one entitled, "notice-medical examination", and the other, "instructions". The document of instructions notifies him of his right to apply for postponement.
Within what length of time?
Under the regulations he is required to apply for postponement within eight clear days of the date of the notice.
He received notice to report within six days.

The minister has given us an explanation about the various classes which have been called up. The other night we heard about conscientious objectors, and to-night we have been hearing about enemy aliens. A great deal of money has been spent by this



War Appropriation-War Services
department in connection with mobilization since the start of the war. The army under the control of the minister has a different system. I do not wish to be unfair. I have described this department as an omnibus department, and I do not think it can be described in any other way. However, in connection with mobilizing men for the army the department has been a flat failure right from the start.
We have had recruiting on again, off again and on again. Aliens and conscientious objectors who are called up seem to be received into the army with kid gloves. The treatment they receive is different from that given to those trainees who were called up two weeks ago. I saw some of them in the union station at Toronto and other places on their way to camps. In one camp in the Toronto district, before the trainees had been in camp twenty-four hours, they were told by coercion that unless they enlisted for active service overseas they would be moved out very shortly to another place. Is there to be one law for the British-born in this country and another for the alien from continental Europe? If these people come to this country and accept the freedom, liberty, rights and privileges of Canada, then when the enemy is at the front door, the side door, the baok door and all the other doors of this country, these people should be compelled to do their duty to the land of their adoption. That is the first duty of any citizen since any country has been a country.
I may not be very good at arithmetic. I may be something like the editor of the Ottawa Citizen who was referred to the other night by an hon. member. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle got into an argument with the minister on the call-ups in Quebec and Ontario, and on arithmetical and geometrical progression and harmonical progressive mathematics over the way in which these particular people were called up. There were 38,000 called up, and 37,000 asked to be excused in one province. It seems to me that the more that are called, the fewer get into the army. There are so many varieties of calls that about the only call I have not heard of being sent out to these men to enlist is a call to the bar. Many are called but few are chosen under the minister's department. The system is an impossible one. How can we win this war and Canada do its duty under the present system, or secure a total war effort? We are now in the sixth month of this year, and not a thing has yet been done to get men into the army. Men are willing voluntarily to go into the air force or the navy, both of which have a 
large waiting list, but there are so many riders, restrictions, exceptions and provisos that the army has been hampered from the start in getting men.
The mother country is wondering what is the matter with Canada. Canada was represented at the imperial conference in 1937 and knew the great danger for our empire there was on both the Atlantic and the Pacific and to the province of Quebec and the maritimes. All the cards were on the table, and Canada knew what was going to happen. Yet we cut down our expenditures until we had no fleet and no air force at all. What did Canada say at that 1937 conference? She held aloof, refused to cooperate with Britain, and said: "We have no commitments. Parliament must decide". The Minister of National War Services himself was one of the main supporters of this policy of neutrality.
That is not true.

A bill standing in his
name was on the order paper six months before the war, declaring that if war came, Canada was bound to be neutral. The bill declaring for isolation came up for second reading on March 31, 1939, and I talked it out. I will read the preamble:
Whereas it is expedient that the status of Canada in time of war should be made clear and declared by the parliament of Canada: Therefore His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
(1) Canada shall not assume the status of a belligerent.
This bill was discussed in the House of Commons, and it was or seemed to be the policy of the government of the day; there is no doubt about that. Why, the Prime Minister himself visited Hitler in 1937 and had a conference with him. I asked what the conference was about, but he was not prepared to say in detail.
The minister the other night said that the North American continent, Canada and the United States, was isolationist. He was and always was. Are we, the British-born, going to sit here in this house and listen to such remarks as were made here last Friday, at a time like this when Great Britain is grappling with the foe and was left to bear the whole brunt of the war for two years and four months alone? After Dunkirk we thought Britain would be invaded and the British empire would be gone; but as Mr. Churchill said, speaking in this house, Britain then had "some neck". We have been sending emissaries and wasting money in publicity all over the United States for the past ten or

fifteen years; we have established an embassy at Washington, all tending to separatism and isolationism. Then we sent deputies to Hollywood, by aeroplane, spending from $40,000 to $60,000 on pictures according to Hollywood to convert the United States to war. Last session congress	carried the
president's army bill by only one vote; the neutrality law was repealed by only fourteen votes in the senate, and that country was until Pearl Harbour isolationist. Canada is not and never was isolationist or for separation. The government was before the war.
If we do not wake up we shall have a Pearl Harbour in the St. Lawrence, while we sit here talking about raising a few men for the army. If it took as long to get twelve men for a jury as it takes under this cumbersome system to get twelve soldiers, there would be veiy few cases tried by jury in this country.
I can tell you that Canada is not going to be talked out of the British empire. Canada will have to be fought out of the British empire. I tell the government of the day: You cannot ride two horses regarding the army any longer. You must line up with the mother country and help Canadargel her~anraTmy now before it is too late next summer. Every sixty seconds to the minute, every sixty minutes to the hour, every twenty-four hours in the day we are approaching the midsummer climax which will decide the fate of the British empire, of the world and of this country and of civilization forever and the fate of religion, freedom and liberty. Yet here we sit day after day since January devising riders, restrictions, provisos and exemptions for this class and that, which make it almost impossible for the minister himself to do his duty of getting men for the army. I think he would like to do it if he could. He was wrong before the war. Handicapped as he is I believe he has done the best he can. But he is hedged about with doubts, provisos and all that kind of thing.
Like the editor of the Ottawa Citizen on the 38,000 called up and 37,000 wanting a stay, I may not understand arithmetic; that is what was said of him here, or of one of the staff of that paper. My hon. friend the member for Qu'Appelle does arithmetic every day, as I see when I go to his office, and he said the other night that he knew something about arithmetic when he had a debate on arithmetic with the minister. I have said before that the House of Commons never wants to be told that two and two make four but would rather be told that two and two do not make five. What is the position with respect to these figures? Thirty-eight thousand in Quebec were called up, received notice to report to the registrar, and 37,000 of
these gentlemen wanted to be postponed and 23,000 of these were allowed a stay. For two years and eight months the war has gone on, and all these gentlemen ask for a postponement. If the war lasted for fifty years there would still be a majority of them wanting postponement. We will never get an army to defend Canada or overseas. If all the arithmetic in the figures tabled is wrong and the headlines in the newspapers are wrong, the information and publicity bureau should be abolished altogether. The information bureau was established before the minister took over his office, I know, but I say that the publicity that has been turned out from the information bureau marks it as the most mischievous institution in this country. That publicity published in Hansard of Friday last leads Britain to believe that the whole north American continent, Canada and the United States before the war, was against her when Britain was bearing the whole brunt of the war for over two years alone. Canada was not for isolation. Last year Britain bore the brunt of the war, and in 1942 Russia is bearing the brunt. Russia, with 2,000,000 men, and -what aid she is getting-JromRhe-allies, a comparatively small amount of equipment, with some help from the Royal Air Force, is attacked by Germany, and Germany now has 3,000,000 German soldiers and 14,000 German tanks. What aid are we giving? Britain is doing well in aiding her with production and an air force.
Are we doing our duty at this fateful hour in the empire's history? What have we done? We had a proposal of mine four years before the war for a national selective registry, but nothing came of it. Then in 1940 we had the registry taken by the minister's department, although he was not in office then. It was a registry taken all over Canada at huge cost. Information was collected showing the number of men of military age. Very little was done about that and the tabulation took too long. Then we had a census, again at a huge cost to this country. Then we had a plebiscite with a lot of information and six weeks of talk, and a stay, and now we have some more registers of the ministry of labour which no doubt will also be committed to the archives with the new selective register- earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust, in the sure and certain hope that they will never be resurrected again as far as this government is concerned. Mr. Churchill said the other month in the British House of Commons that humbug plays a large part in our democratic bodies. Well, I think he must have been in this chamber and had a look round; he would have found considerable evidence to prove the correctness of his aphorism.

Never were there so many who knew so little about so much, especially as it applies to the army and to the minister and his isolation policy of 1939. This proposal to establish a publicity bureau in the United States reminds me that the government had a great advocate of publicity sent in an expeditionary force to the United States, in Mr. L. W. Brockington; that gentleman went up and down the United States, Washington-minded telling them, "King George did not declare war for us; we declared war for him." That is the kind of separatist and isolationist talk for which we are invited to pay under this minister with the Atlantic situation as it is to-day, and radio talk and propaganda. The people voted for a total war to beat Hitler.
The Minister of Finance said the other night that there is something wrong with the House of Commons. What is wrong with the house is that the government of the day want us to be nothing more than a lot of yes-men and nodders. They have removed control by the high court of parliament over expenditures and any control by the auditor general. Yet we are responsible for how all this money is being spent, much of it on publicity and information bureaux, on the plebiscite, and so forth. Not one dollar of the estimates has been passed yet this year on the seventy-sixth day of our sittings.
The government is not taking the right way to get an army. The manner in which the quotas are established and enforced is very unfair to Ontario. I had a return tabled, and it shows that Ontario is contributing a larger part of the army, navy and air force than is any other province.
That is not so.

The people of this country want the government to get on with the war and a total war effort. The yes vote showed the unanimous desire of the great majority of the people to cooperate to the last man and the last dollar with the mother country. When all is said and done, everything we in this country have to-day of freedom, civilization and liberty we owe to the mother country, and the United States is in the same position. Were it not for the heroic stand of the British people after Dunkirk the war was lost and the United States, on this continent, would long ago have had to make peace with the axis powers, who by then might have been in Washington. But we can take one leaf out of the book of the United States, by learning how she enforces the draft against all, and deals with aliens and those who disobey the draft laws. There is not one law 
there for the rich and another for the poor. All must obey it. Moreover, in the United States everybody is expected to salute the flag, and there is only one flag and one anthem. There is only one flag in this country, the union jack; there is only one anthem, the national anthem. Our United States friends require every citizen, young and old, to salute the stars and stripes and their anthem, and to give prompt obedience to their draft laws, while we in this country sit here putting in provisos, exceptions, exemptions, and all that kind of thing.
I do not know that I can say anything further. I am sorry to have detained the committee so long; it was not my intention to have spoken, but I feel I should state that in my belief what was said last Friday in this chamber disheartens the people of the motherland at the darkest hour of the w*ar. That Canada, the senior dominion, takes the position expressed by her official spokesmen of the cabinet in the House of Commons causes us to be compared with countries which were isolationist and separatist before the war. I doubt whether we would have had war if this dominion had done its duty at the last imperial conference, instead of urging disarmament.
In my opinion this department has outlived its usefulness. What has this information and publicity branch accomplished for all the money that has been spent? After all, the worst informed people are the people of Canada. Quite a number of Canadian newspapers do not report the proceedings of this house. We cannot blame them. Some of them think the proceedings are not worth reporting; that is a matter for them to decide; but I will say that if the mint of money which has gone to the publicity branch and the information bureau had been spent on the press in getting proper information to the public through the press, the results would have been quite different. Our newspapers are interesting and entertaining; they have fulfilled a fine function in this war mostly at their own expense, and without cost to the government. The work which one Toronto newspaper did for British victims, in educating the people of Ontario and all Canada, was one of the most cheering things which has greeted the mother country since the war began, and shows that the heart of Canada, at least, is sound and is with Britain to the end. If we had publicity of that kind in this country and in the United States I would not object to it, because in America they owe a great debt of gratitude to Britain for the fleet which has protected their shores, and but for which they would have been subjected to blockade and blackouts, and have suffered the ravages of Hitlerism two years ago.

The Prime Minister,
speaking in the house on July 12, 1940, in moving the second reading of the bill setting up the Department of National War Services, outlined the general scope of this department. He said, as reported at page 1571 of Hansard of that year:
The department will also undertake the initiation and promotion of voluntary effort in new directions, in immediate furtherance of our war effort and to enable Canada to make in the most effective and efficient manner the necessary economic and social adjustments to meet domestic problems arising out of the war.
I know that the minister in charge of this department has to do with things of the mind which might not appear to be as spectacular as the building of ships, aerodromes, tanks and the other commodities necessary in connection with the prosecution of the war. Nevertheless a very important role must be filled by the minister if the Canadian people are to understand clearly the issues which are at stake and are to be persuaded to do whatever is necessary to carry this war through to a successful conclusion.
To-night I should like to discuss one field of activity where, to date, I feel that the government has been lax. In connection with the consumption of liquor in Canada the government has failed to do the necessary work in informing our people of the tremendous losses in production which go hand in hand with the increasing manufacture and consumption of liquor.
Mr. E. P. Taylor, one of the dollar-a-year men associated with the government, and president of Canadian Breweries Limited, was interviewed by the Toronto Globe arid Mail after he returned from the old country about a year ago, and he is reported as saying:
A lot of the non-essential industrial activities (in Canada) of different kinds will gradually have to be curtailed as fast as we can obtain machinery to produce war materials.
He thought that Canadians were not taking the war seriously enough and urged that they must forgo luxuries for guns and tanks and aeroplanes.
That was in February, 1941. In February, 1942, Toronto Saturday Night devoted a full page to telling just exactly what Mr. Taylor's firm is doing to carry out the objective that he outlined while speaking to the Globe ajid Mail. The annual report, which is signed by E. P. Taylor as president, boasts of this fact:
Your company has for several months been carrying on an extensive export business to the British forces in the theatres of war.
Another paragraph:
After providing for depreciation and other charges, including income and excess profits taxes, the net profit for the year amounts to $570,570.11, in comparison with $525,032.78, in
the previous year. Dividends were paid on the preference shares at the full rate of $3 per share. . . .
Further extensive improvements were made to several of the company's plants.
Another paragraph mentions:
Your directors are now putting forward a proposal for the elimination of the arrears of dividends on the preference shares, which is embodied in a by-law to be submitted to the holders of preference shares and the shareholders as a whole at separate meetings as indicated in the accompanying notice.
I wonder if anyone ever heard of men in industry who were unemployed for several years being able to take advantage of present situation to secure the arrears of wages which they did not receive. Yet Mr. Taylor indicates that his company plans to pay now the dividends that were not paid during the depression.
In the Brewers Magazine of May, 1941, there appears this amazing statement:
One of the finest things that could have happened to the brewing industry was the insistence of high ranking officers to make beer available at army camps. . . . The opportunity presented to the brewing industry by this measure is so obvious that it is superfluous to go into it in detail. Here is a chance for brewers to cultivate a taste for beer in millions of young men who will eventually constitute the largest beer consuming section of our population.
Apparently, with companies like Canadian Breweries Limited and their subsidiaries and the Brewers Magazine carrying on such vicious propaganda, it can scarcely be left to the good intentions of private individuals to see that the necessary restrictions are carried into effect.
In July, 1940, representatives of nearly all the churches in Canada and the temperance organizations waited on the government and made four concrete proposals:
1.	That the sale of alcoholic beverages in taverns, beer rooms, wine shops, etc., be discontinued and that sale of such beverages be confined entirely to government-owned liquor stores.
2.	That sale from government liquor stores be permitted only between the hours of 3 o'clock in the afternoon and 8 o'clock in the evening and on week days only.
3.	That all advertising of liquor in Canada be forbidden except in the place of sale.
4.	That when the request in item 1 is implemented, an order issue from the Department of Defence closing all wet canteens in military establishments.
Seven months after this delegation waited on the government and made their proposals I asked in the House of Commons on February 19, 1941, as reported at page 826 of Hansard of that year:
Has the government adopted any change in policy in connection with the manufacture and sale of liquor under the War Measures Act?

According to the laws of Ontario a magazine of this sort could not be published in this province, because of its liquor advertisements. I do not know whether hon. members are familiar with this magazine, but it presents a subtle type of propaganda. It is an extremely attractive magazine. Mr. Taylor
has secured - a capable editor, who has obtained from contributors articles of interest, and many interesting pictures are displayed. On the last page of the magazine we find an attractive advertisement telling what Sir John Carling's Red Cap ale will do for you. Turning to the next page we find a large advertisement in connection with Booth's gin. On another page there is an advertisement for Dewar's Scotch whisky, and on the next page an advertisement for Four Roses, a Canadian whisky. Then we see, "Have a Guinness To-Day!" Apparently they are able to find space to bring this choice beverage across from the other side, and it is apparently one of the popular drinks in Canada. On the next page there is an advertisement for Vat 69; I do not know what that is. The next advertisement is for Seagram's V.O., which is called the perfect whisky. Turning the page we find an attractive half-page advertisement for Three Castles whisky and London Club gin, and on the very next page another attractive half-page advertisement for Sir Robert Burnett's London dry gin. Hon. members will see from the attractive colouring of this advertisement that it has been prepared by one of our best artists. So we see that large sums of money are spent in order to encourage our people to consume these liquors. Another advertisement is for Gilbey's gin; and then covering two pages, is an advertisement for White Label ale. Again the minister smiles, but I submit that with Canada at war it is unfair to allow advertisements of this type to appear in a hundred thousand copies of this magazine which are on the news stands every month, in order to encourage our young people to consume liquor.
I understand the procedure is that the editorial offices and circulation department are in Toronto, in the Concourse building, 100 Adelaide street west; all correspondence regarding advertising is directed to be sent to this address. I understand that most of the printing is done in Toronto by two well-known publishers; then the material is shipped to Montreal, and the complete magazine is mailed from Montreal back to the news stands. In this way it is possible to see that advertisements of this kind go into the homes of our Canadian people, so that the increase in the consumption of these liquors may continue.
I have heard criticism as a result of churches in Canada being asked to cooperate with various government departments, and then when they desired paid advertisements for their papers they have not been very successful. But I find the government has been quite generous to the New World. There are several advertisements inserted in this issue

To bring tea from Ceylon and India, to bring coffee from South America, ships must cross oceans infested with submarines. Since sugar rationing was first introduced, the shipping situation has become more serious. The danger to ships and lives has increased. Consequently it has now become necessary to reduce the sugar ration from f lb. to i lb. per week per person.
The Canadian people are not objecting to cutting down their sugar, tea and coffee. They realize that one of the most valuable services being performed is that of the men who go out to the sea to risk their lives in order to keep open the channels of commerce. But I think it disgraceful that we should be able to find shipping space for unlimited quantities of liquor while we have to restrict our consumption of coffee, tea and sugar, and that so far no attempt has been made to get the Canadian people to restrict their consumption of liquor.
In view of the situation I have outlined; in view of the alarming increase in the consumption of liquor in every province of Canada, I wonder if the minister would not give further consideration to this matter. I wonder if he will not admit that this now has become a national problem and that, regardless of what he may have said or what may have been done in the past, some steps should be taken, in the first place to see that advertisements of this type will be discontinued for the duration of the war and, in the second place, that our people will be encouraged to reduce their consumption of liquor.
