I should like to follow what was said by the hon. member who has just spoken, and refer particularly to two branches under the Department of National War Services. May I tell the minister that I have always had a deep respect for him. I believe he is in earnest, takes care of his department and in some branches has able assistants. I pay special tribute to Mr. Justice Davis and to General LaFleche. My colleagues in the house know the feelings I have for General LaFleche; I have great admiration for him. Then, in my humble view Major Benoit is also an able man.
Whatever anyone else may think of the importance of the Department of National War Services, in my opinion that department is equal in importance to any of the war departments. This is my reason for making that statement: The government has at its disposal some wonderful agencies under the supervision of that department. I have in mind particularly the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which is under the control of the minister to as great an extent as any semiindependent corporation could be. It lives upon the taxes paid by owners of radio sets.
I wonder if the best use is made of that agency, both within and without the country.
Inside our boundaries the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation could do excellent work not only for what is called national unity, but also for the union of all Canadians of goodwill, especially in times like these. Of course good men are required to operate the corporation.
Then there is a further branch of the department which at times has to operate with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and also with the bureau of information. I refer to the censors branch, which has been centralized under the minister. In addition to the minister's function of calling men under the National Resources Mobilization Act, he has a duty so important and so great as to consume the whole of his time.
Is the information bureau operating properly? The minister is not responsible for its organization, because it was in operation when he became head of the department. He had to take it as it was. I ask the minister now to place on Hansard an up-to-date list of the staff of the information bureau, showing the occupation and salary of each member of the personnel. That is the first step. I complain that the cooperation between the information bureau and the censors is not close enough. Of course in times past the censors were not all under the minister. A reorganization was made not long ago, and now the two agencies are under the same minister. But that is not enough. They must work together. The information bureau must give a lead, and the check must be by the censors.
I have heard a good deal about the present head of the censors. It is said that he is an able man, and I give him the benefit of the doubt. I have no reason to complain about him, but his functions are of the utmost importance. He should proceed, not only with scissors in hand but by way of giving a lead to the newspapers and to Canadians who speak inside and outside the country. An effort should be made to make the bureau of the greatest possible help.
What should be done by the bureau? It is a Canadian bureau, and charity begins at home. It should serve the Canadian people first by giving us some idea of what orders in council of a legislative nature are passed by the government by virtue of the War Measures Act. Where is the member of parliament who can read, analyse, check and note all the orders in council of a legislative nature passed daily by the government? It is impossible. This information bureau should show its usefulness by keeping members informed on this legislation of a special nature which we cannot analyse from a study of the



War Appropriation-War Services
Canada Gazette. This afternoon an hon. member asked about the publication of these orders in council in book form. Already we have had five of these books, but some orders in council are amended and others are repealed. Part of the work of this information bureau should be done by jurists, and these orders in council should be issued in loose-leaf form.
The bureau of information should not be a clearing house for just the publicity of one department, the Department of Munitions and Supply. It should be a clearing house for all departments. It should give information to the people so that they may know what they have to do in order to live up to these governmental regulations. That would be easy to do provided the minister selects competent men to head the branch. The branch will justify its existence if the work is properly done, and I think hon. members will be grateful to the minister if such a change is made. A number of orders in council were published as an appendix to the Votes and Proceedings of March 24. No one knew the tenor of those orders until after eleven o'clock in the morning, and yet they had been in effect from the previous Monday. No one outside the members of the government knew what they were, and yet they affected the lives of the population of Canada. One will answer that that is the practice; but whether it is or not, I think it is an abuse.
Years ago the Department of National Revenue used to publish a monthly account of exports and imports as between the United Kingdom and Canada and as between Canada and foreign countries. This has been stopped under the pretext of economy, but we now receive certain information from the information bureau. The information put out in French is simply silly. It means nothing at all; it is just childishness and is of no use to us. All that we in the province of Quebec ask is that we be served in the same way as our fellow citizens who speak the English language. Why should- we be given this sort of information that is of no use?
The information bureau could give advice over the radio about health, diet and so on. This could be given by experts, other than those who belong to the medical profession.
I am sure that this will satisfy my hon. friend who made some apt remarks about what has been done. The information bureau should not give false ideas to other departments. Here is an example of the silly things that are put out. This is entitled "A Call to Arms," and is put out on the most expensive paper and signed by the Minister of National Defence. I say this is silly because of what 
happened when it was published. Several men in my county wanted to enlist, and I went with them to the armoury where the man in charge of enlistments was supposed to be. The very room in which this poster was displayed was locked. These boys with me wanted: to enlist, but the door was well locked and nobody could get in.
No shortage of paper there.

This was asking boys to enlist, but the door was closed. Then there was something else. I refer to the totem pole that was carried across Canada, that thing called a victory torch which was sent to England with the first money that was obtained in the victory loan campaign last year. The money was used for the expenses of a trip in a bomber to carry that totem pole. Mr. Churchill looked astounded when he received it at No. 10 Downing street. Things like that are no good. We have a call to arms, a call to enlist, and when boys go to enlist they find no one there and the door looked against them. The first money obtained from the savings of the Canadian people is used to transport that totem pole from British Columbia to Halifax and then across the Atlantic by bomber. I do not blame the minister, I blame the man who had that silly idea. I am sure it came from the information bureau. It appeared to me like a bit of idolatry.
The idea originated in British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No; it did not. It came from the victory loan committee.

I do not want to hurt my hon. friend because I am in full sympathy with him. I shed tears when I thought of that.
There is something else, and here is where there should be intervention by the censorship bureau. It should tell important military men who are in charge of the districts of Quebec and Montreal to shut up and not enter into any competition in eloquence as they do, only, as we say in French, to "Mettre les pieds dans les plats"-"put their feet in dishes."
Another thing should be done by the censor. Here is another kind of foolish propaganda that came from the national plebiscite committee. It is signed by Florian Fortin. I have already complained about it. It was printed and widely distributed during the plebiscite campaign:
What shall we think of persons who vote "no" under the pretext that they do not love England.
It is silly. Why put such ideas in the heads of Canadian people?

War Appropriation-War Services
Another thing that the censors should do is to forbid government agencies from sending out copies of articles from a stinky paper in Montreal called Le Jour.
I did not hear what the hon. gentleman called the paper.

Stinky-malodorous. All that sort of thing works not only on the mind of my good friend the leader of the opposition but on the minds of some journalists. For instance, I received not long ago an article published in a Woodstock paper, the editor of which is at present on leave, working for the wartime prices and trade board. Underneath the article is this note:
Suggest you get all your "no" voters out in rowboats to locate the U-boats.
Very witty! It also works on the editorial staff of our dear local paper, the Ottawa Citizen, which says:
Since Jean-Frangois Pouliot and other members from the Lower St. Lawrence don't faney going abroad to defend their country, wasn't it accommodating of the sub to come all the way over and make faces at them on their own door-step!
Is it not very clever? That is the consequence of such propaganda.
But it works on somebody else. It works on one who cannot sing, "Yes, we have no bananas," because he is the Orange leader of Ontario, the Ontario Grand Master, Mr. J. W. Carson. The headline says:
Quebec stand deplored by Orange leader- "Unbelievable" Ontario Grand Master tells gathering.
The article goes on to say:
The grand master repeated "our long-standing protest" against the "persistent and insistent" attempts to elevate the French language to a parity with English "and more particularly against the practice of the federal government in circulating, indiscriminately throughout the dominion, publications and forms printed in both languages."
I never knew that, but I am indulgent to the head of the Orangemen just on account of the silliness of the propaganda that was put out by the information bureau, because I understand he was deceived by it.
There is one of our colleagues who said once that those who did not agree with him were inspired by Hitler or something like that. I want to be indulgent to him for the same reason.
Another of our lady colleagues spoke of Quebec Quislings. I understand that she also was led into error by the same sort of propaganda.
I do not care what is said about me. For instance, an Ottawa paper called me a noxious
pest. I am quite indifferent to that. Another paper, this one from western Ontario, said:
By far the worst offence was that of Mr. Jean-Frangois Pouliot, who since 1924 has been creating scenes of disturbance in the house, mainly by launching virulent attacks against men who, not being members, have no means of defending themselves. He followed his old tactics again in his latest outburst.
I do not care about that.
Another Toronto paper dedicated an editorial to myself, headed "Buffoonery in parliament." I do not care at all about that. Another weekly Ontario paper said something else, just to frighten me, referring to something I had said regarding the Minister of National Defence. He said he would stop what I was doing. I do not know whether these articles were inspired or not. This one is from a weekly, printed on shiny paper. It says:
Mr. Pouliot is at the same time too much of an egoist and too much of a comedian to be a reliable colleague in any ministry.
I am indifferent to all that, and I know the censor should not intervene in such cases because it is simply the expression of one individual's opinion.
But this sort of propaganda has a bad effect. It turns the minds of some people. I will give one example. It dates back to a year ago. It is a very bad letter that I received. I made a speech here on February 21, 1941. Mr. Lapointe spoke on February 24, and then on February 26 a letter was sent to me from Toronto. Mr. Lapointe told me in front of one of my colleagues that this letter should be read. I have already given a copy of it to the Prime Minister, also to Mr. Godbout, Premier of Quebec, and to Mr. Duplessis. The letter shows the turn of mind of some people, and I am sure that there is not a member of the house who will not be scandalized by what is said in it. We hear about national unity. Of course, that must work on both sides. I have already said that in any country where there is a minority the minority has always to suffer from the greed of the majority to govern, and that characteristic goes back to the far-away ages. As we say in French, "Diviser un petit peuple"-"Divide to rule." That was said about twenty centuries ago, and it is still true. This is deplorable. The following letter was addressed to J. F. Pouliot, M.P., Ottawa, Parliament buildings, and mailed at Toronto, February 27, 1941, 9.30 p.m. Here it is, and I will lay the original on the table:
715 Palmerston Avenue,
Toronto, February 26, 1941.
Dear Half-Breed:
You were right when you told Mr. Ralston the other day that you have been here for a

War Appropriation-War Services
long time. It is a long time since the priest chased and raped the squaw and you were the result, also Lapointe, Duplessis, Godbout, how you half-breeds like to blow.
You should hang your head in shame and never tell anybody that you belong to the French cattle.
Look at those dirty French traitors in France; it is a laugh to hear you dogs talking about culture. They sold out to the Germans thinking they were going to save their own dirty necks, but you see what traitors get. But they cannot help being traitors. It is born in them just like you dogs in Quebec. What we need in Canada is a nice little war to clean out all you cattle along with the arch louse and traitor, Mackenzie King. The war is not over yet but I would sooner fight you half-breeds than I would the Germans.
Yours,
Joe Smith.
I find by the 1940 Toronto city directory that the two persons who are indicated as residing at the above address, 715 Palmerston Avenue, are Jack Woulter and Frank Schicht. That is not helpful.
At a time when our publicity was not going well in the United States, we have here the sort of uncensored publicity which was published in the Montreal Gazette:
We must have victory. You must vote "Yes!"
This publicity is sponsored by plebiscite committees of the province of Quebec.
I wonder if that was paid for by the government. It is not the way to have national unity in this country. Here is another advertisement which was published on April 25, and was not censored:
How would Hitler vote?
Pause for a moment and ask yourself this question: If Hitler had a vote on the plebiscite, how would he mark his ballot? Your good sense tells you he would say "no". If you vote "no" or if you don't vote at all, you are helping Hitler.
We hear that we have a bad name in the United States. That is not surprising when one reflects upon what is said about those who do not agree with the government on this question. I have one other exhibit; it is from Time, a Luce publication, of May 11, 1942, and on page 30 it reproduces a photograph of a sign:
Hitler voterait non sur le plebiscite.
Comment voterez-vous?
"Hitler would vote no on the plebiscite. How will you vote?" It is headed, "Quebec Posters. The little one says, 'If you would avoid conscription, vote no.' " This is the kind of publicity we have in the United States. It is just a continuation of the publicity we have had in this country. I have never understood why the censor did not stop it. It is important to preserve national unity in this country. We hear fine speeches about 
national unity. Speeches do not count; it is acts that count, and the necessary act should be to stop such publications, especially of an official nature.
As an example of the kind of publicity which we should have in the United States, I will refer to a publication which I hold in my hand, and which is widely circulated on this continent and even, at least formerly, in Europe. There was a French edition of Vogue published in Paris and an English edition published in London. It is a ladies' magazine, and it is read throughout the world. I do not know whether even now they have not a Spanish edition for south America. Here is what is written in the May issue by a distinguished and brilliant member of our own press gallery, who has international fame, and who, especially since the publication of his last book on this country, is nearly as well and favourably known in the United States as in Canada. I refer to Mr. Bruce Hutchison of Vancouver, who has written a story, "While I was in Quebec." It is a story of a young man who becomes a member of parliament.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: OrdeT, please. I should like to draw to the attention of the hon. member that when he refers to a publication relating to the expenditure of SI,500,000,000 by the government there may be some relevancy in his remarks, but I cannot see the connection of the matter before the committee now with an article written by a gentleman in the magazine Vogue which has nothing to do with the expenditure by the government of the amount of money which is now sought to be obtained.
Well, sir, we were just speaking of the information bureau.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes, but exactly on that point, anything which is published by the department and is directly or indirectly connected with the expenditure of the moneys voted by parliament would be in order. But we cannot enter, on a discussion of a resolution of this kind, into an analysis or a criticism of an article published by somebody else in Vogue.

Well, sir, I will explain what my purpose is in mentioning that. I was complaining that the information bureau was not doing useful work in this country and outside. I was complaining of propaganda which was going on outside which was not checked by the censor, and I was showing how the Americans could be favourably impressed with Canada by able and worthy propaganda. I am well aware that Vogue is a woman's magazine, but it has incorporated Vanity Fair, which was a magazine for both

War Appropriation-War Services
men and women, and contained serious articles, and this article contains a few remarks which are an antidote to the poison that was published in Lije. That is why I want to show that a censoring and an information bureau should take advantage of what is published by Mr. Hutchison in Vogue to follow that example. My quotation is not long, just a few lines.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Very well.

It reads:
This, though no one here realized it, was the symbol of a strange fact in the life of America and a basic fact in Canada. This was the French race, a third of the Canadian nation, making its will felt with the majority by skill, by persistence, by a hard common sense hidden under a smile and the shrug of a shoulder. This was the emergence, out of the rich Quebec soil, of another leader, whence so many had come since Champlain's time. And in Lucien's marriage to this blond girl, who spoke no French, one could see the hope that some day the two great races would unite, creating a race still greater.
This is the kind of thing which should go from Canada to the United States, and Mr. Hutchison rendered a valuable service to all Canada by writing in that way in a United States magazine with such a wide circulation.
Of course, no French Canadian will contend that we have all perfection and all virtue. We do not pretend that we are any better than our English-speaking fellow citizens, but it is merely a legitimate pride to contend that we are just as good, and what we want is to have the opportunity to show to the majority of the Canadian people that the province of Quebec is not behind any province in the *war effort. I claim that for the people of my province; I insist upon that for them. I hope, according to the news I have received, that in the near future I shall be able to give that information to the English-speaking population of this country. I am sure that my fellow-citizens of a different origin are open-minded enough to take it objectively, without prejudice, and to judge as they deserve those who are responsible for the kind of propaganda which has given them such a false impression of good citizens who are just as anxious as they are to see this country prosper and to win the war.'

I should like to say a
few words in connection with the information department under the minister. I believe that the situation which we now face in Canada and the grave domestic condition with which we are confronted are in no small measure due to the failure of the government's information service. Since the war broke out there has been, I believe, an opportunity for
the information service to place the issues of this war in a manner which would have won a larger measure of support from all the people of Canada, had those issues been properly presented. I do not propose to go into details; but I sometimes think, after having read the translations of some of the talks, for example, that have been put over the French network in this country, that a great deal better could have been done. I have wondered why the ordinary common masses of the people could not have talked to the ordinary common masses of the people overseas, and vice versa. I believe that probably one of the ways in which the people of English-speaking Canada have been brought to an understanding of the issues of this war is through the talks we have had from fishermen, miners, farm labourers, and ordinary housewives in Great Britain, over the radio, in newsreels and by means of other broadcasts of that description which we have had from overseas.
I believe that we have suffered a great loss in Canada because we ourselves have not had the means of exchanging with the people across the seas our ideas for theirs. I have regretted ever since the war broke out, yes, before the war broke out, that we have not had a short-wave transmitter which would have enabled us and our compatriots of all national origins to speak directly to similar peoples across the seas. We have in this country Germans who are as much opposed to Hitler as we are, and with more reason. We have Czechs happily settled in this country free to follow their own ways of life. We have a Canadian population speaking the French language who still maintain many of the attributes of old France, and I am of opinion that the French-Canadian farmer speaking directly to the peasant of France would be better understood than almost any other medium we have. Broadcasts that are coming from Vichy and from Paris at the present time under German control, directed to our Canadian compatriots who speak the French language, say of course that the condition in France is far better than we know it to be, and misrepresent the intentions of the majority of the people of this country, the English-speaking majority, to our Canadian friends who speak the French language. If you follow, as I have followed, some of the broadcasts-not in French, for I do not understand the language sufficiently well; but I have read the English translations-you will realize the degree of difficulty that we encounter because our people cannot speak directly to the people across the seas and tell them of the actual conditions of democratic freedom that exist in Canada. The same

War Appropriation-War Services
applies to the people who speak Polish and other languages-Norwegian, Dutch, Danish and so on, the languages of the peoples of oppressed Europe.
I believe that one of the finest things we could have done in the prosecution of the war from the point of view of the Canadian citizen, the unity of our people and the interpretation of Canadian, north American and British ideals, would have been done through properly organized short-wave programmes. Though we have a radio committee sitting and I am a member of that committee, I realize at the moment that we are discussing the appropriation of funds for this department; but by the time the radio committee rises, the budget debate will in all probability have been concluded and there will have been no opportunity to press for the establishment of a powerful short-wave transmitter for this dominion. If Great Britain were invaded -and of course it is not improbable that some attempt may still be made by para^-chutists to invade and seek to control a part of Great Britain-if any part of Britain were taken even temporarily by the enemy, if the British Broadcasting Corporation's transmitter at Daventry were put out of operation, there would be no powerful station within the British commonwealth that could speak to the rest of the world.
The parliamentary committee in 1938 recommended something of the sort. It said:
Your committee was impressed with the importance of the establishment at an early date of a high-power short-wave broadcasting station. Such a station your committee believes would be a great utility in interpreting and advertising Canada abroad and in facilitating an exchange of programmes between Canada and other broadcasting systems. Canada, your committee has been informed, is the only major training nation without such facilities, and it is submitted that this should be financed as a national project operated and controlled by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It should be a public utility and free from partisan control.
So that in 1938 the committee which sat at that time was strongly of opinion that we should have a short-wave broadcasting station for this dominion.
Was that ever concurred in by the House of Commons?
The report was presented but, as usual with our reports, I do not think it was formally adopted.
If it were, it would be a command.
I do not think it was ever formally adopted.
The government allowed it to die.

Nothing was done about it, and in 1939 this was a recommendation of another committee:
The committee of last year emphasized the importance of establishing, at as early a date as possible, a high-power short-wave broadcasting station, financed as a national undertaking but operated and controlled by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as an integral part of its system.
There you have a reaffirmation of the belief that this should be done.

But that
was only a committee of parliament. Why was parliament not asked to pass upon it?

I think the leader of
the opposition knows quite well that reports are presented here and then more or less forgotten. Unless the government brings forward the necessary appropriation, nothing is done about the matter. To-day when we send a minister of the crown, as we sent the Minister of Trade and Commerce and members of his department, to South America on a good-will tour to promote trade and good feeling between ourselves and the South American countries, all that effort is lost if we are unable to follow up what he has done. A short-wave broadcasting station in Canada could convey to our South American friends the atmosphere of this country. It could tell them what this country was doing, both in peace and in war. I venture to suggest that to some extent the British have been a little suspect in South America, because they were looked upon as being imperialistic, financially, in their aims. The American, the Yankee trader if you will, has been suspect in South America because he has been looked upon as an even sharper trader and perhaps a greater potential imperialist than even the Britisher. But we in Canada have had no such reputation. We are a small nation, with no designs on anyone. We do not seek to dominate any part of the globe, either the isles of the sea or in South America. I believe we could have done much to bring the countries of South America a little nearer to us in this time of stress and difficulty if we had been able to speak directly from Canada to the peoples of South America.
To put it on a more prosaic ground, we have the matter of trade and commerce. With the way in which the world is disorganized to-day, even after the war is over Canada may find it difficult to obtain the raw materials she needs and to dispose of many of the commodities which she produces. The good-will of consuming nations in South America may be of very great value to us. Let us not

War Appropriation-War Services
forget also that ever since the war broke out South America has been under a barrage of propaganda from the axis nations. I have a fairly powerful short-wave set myself, and often when I get home at night I tune in on the short-wave stations. I am amazed at the number of wave-lengths carrying programmes in Portuguese to Brazil and in Spanish to the other countries of South America, from Berlin, Rome and recently from Paris. We have had nothing to counteract that propaganda except the British stations, which sometimes have difficulty in being heard across the seas, and United States stations. As I said before, unforunately from time to time United States interests in South America have not been regarded in altogether the friendly way in which our own interests have been regarded there.
So I am suggesting that even at this late date the government should consider making the necessary appropriation, or authorizing the broadcasting corporation to make the necessary appropriation out of any surplus it may have, to construct a short-wave station at the earliest possible date. I have learned that it is not impossible, even now, to set up a short-wave radio transmitting station. I understand that there is still at least one transmitter available. Incidentally I have also been told-and the minister may correct me if my information is wrong-that as recently as last autumn the government or the corporation was negotiating with regard to such a transmitter. I believe that one of the great companies has offered to assemble and have in operation within a year a short-wave transmitter, at a cost of some 1500,000. That seems a great deal of money, but when we consider that we are appropriating $2,000,000,000 for various war expenditures $500,000 is not a relatively large amount. Indeed, we can easily spend $500,000 on pamphlets, leaflets and literature of other kinds, and lose the advantage from it in a very short space of time, whereas a powerful short-wave transmitter would be a permanent asset to this country both in time of war and in time of peace. Even if it cost, as I understand it would, in the neighbourhood of $150,000 a year to operate-
About $500,000 a year.

I understand $150,000 would be much nearer the figure. I have heard the other figure mentioned also, but my information is that it would cost much less than $500,000. But supposing it did cost the government of this country $500,000 a year to convey to the rest of the world information with regard to Canada; to convey Canada, as it were, to the rest of the world.
That wowld not be a very large sum of money. The value of the good-will resulting would be immeasurably greater than the amount that would be spent. So I am urging upon the government to-night that this matter be considered this year, and that Canada be given a voice across the world. Australia has a short-wave transmitter. It is not very powerful, but Australia is fortunate in having even a 25,00(Lwatt transmitter at this time, for we are privileged occasionally to hear the voices of her statesmen speaking to the United States and the rest of the world. Britain, as I said before, has two transmitters, one of 100,000 watts and the other of 50,000 watts. If anything should happen to those transmitters, Britain would have no voice sufficiently powerful to talk to the rest of the world on behalf of the British commonwealth. It is true that Canadians have been able to broadcast good-will and other messages from time to time through station WRUL at Boston, the world radio university station, but that happens only infrequently. If we had a transmitter, not only could our own people speak to our allies across the sea but some of the outstanding figures from other countries who are now exiles in Canada could speak to their people as well. For example, teaching in the university of Montreal to-day is a great scientist from France, a man who was at one time a member of one of the French governments, serving as under-secretary of state. He was a radical socialist in politics. Lest anyone might misunderstand, may I explain that a radical socialist, before the fall of France-although the name may sound rather forbidding-was a very moderate sort of Liberal. He was just a little to the left of the Republican party.
Not like these Liberals?
Oh, no, not a bit like these Liberals-
Possibly these are radical socialists.
-because they are not very much less Conservative than the Conservative party.
Do not spoil an otherwise good speech by being trapped into anything like that.

Well, the temptation was almost irresistible.
We could use men of this description; and I am therefore urging upon the government that this should be done.

There is one other point I should like to mention before taking my seat, and that is one I raised in the house a short time ago. I do not believe in the suppression of free discussion. I do not believe the press should be interfered with, even in war time, except, of course, that it should not be allowed to publish information which would be of value to the enemy. In Canada I think we may all be proud of the fact that, without a great deal of censorship our own press has voluntarily looked after that angle of its news and of the war effort.
The other afternoon, however, I had occasion to refer to a publication being published in this country by an alien of enemy nationality. It will be noticed that I have not said he is an enemy alien-because I do not believe he is. I describe him as an alien of enemy nationality. I am referring, of course, to the publication of what is known as the "Voice of Austria". A day or two after I made the reference in the house, a bitter attack was lodged by Doctor Franz Klein, editor of the "Voice of Austria" in this country. I went to some trouble in trying to find out if there was any basis for the attack on Doctor Redler, and I have something I should like to place on record, just to keep the record straight, from the Austrian national committee. May I say that the Austrian national committee in New York consists of exiled Austrians of all shades of opinion, right from the monarchists through to the social democrats and the socialists of old Austria.
The Austrian national committee comprises forty of these outstanding Austrians, among whom are two former federal ministers, one former under-secretary of state for foreign affairs, a number of university professors now teaching in the United States and world-famous Austrians like Franz Werfel and Bruno Walter, the great conductor. I have before me a resolution passed by a special meeting of this organization and adopted unanimously on May 16 at their plenary meeting in New York. I should like to quote it:
The plenary assembly entrusts the executive board to take all the necessary steps in order to make it perfectly clear that:
1.	The Austrian natibnal committee has nothing whatsoever to do with. the attacks published in the "Voice of Austria" against statesmen of allied nations;
2.	The Austrian national committee most energetically rejects the attacks published by the editor of this magazine against one of the members of the Austrian national committee.
That is Doctor Redler.
Furthermore, it was agreed that the executive board should bring the resolution concerning

the "Voice of Austria" to the attention of all the interested foreign authorities, in particular, the British and Czechoslovak.
I place that on record because of the injury which might have been done to Doctor Redler who is, I believe, in every way a man with a very line record in the Austrian democratic movement, and who is living in exile in this country. I would suggest this, that when we are carefully supervising papers issued even by our own citizens, as we are in some instances, most careful supervision ought to be given to a publication published by one who is not only not a citizen of this country, but who is of origin the same as that of our enemies. The publication to which I have referred is published in New York, and for some reason Doctor Klein transfers himself to Canada with the result that just lately the paper has been published here. I wanted to place that matter on record because of other things which have been said recently.
It was my wish to bring these several points to the attention of the committee while the minister was before us, and I should like to hear him say to-night if consideration can be given to the establishment of a powerful shortwave station in this country. If consideration is given, I should hope that we may obtain the remaining transmitter which, I am told, is available, and use it for the present and future benefit of Canada and for the immediate war effort of the united nations.
I should like to express my appreciation of the able manner in which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has urged the erection of a short-wave broadcasting station.

You will never get
through your department this way.

The subject has been and still is under consideration by the government. There is not complete agreement on the subject of a short-wave station, but I may say personally to the hon. member that I was very glad indeed to hear his advocacy of something which I think would be of great value to this country, not only at this time but in the post-war period, when Canada should be one of the great nations of the world.
Censorship is another matter which comes under my charge. It operates in a variety of ways, and in respect of various things. It has never been the policy in Canada, in Great Britain or in the United States to discuss the manner in which censorship operates. Generally speaking, the purpose of censorship is twofold. First, its purpose is to prevent information which might be useful to the enemy

War Appropriation-War Services
reaching the enemy and, second, its purpose is to acquire information from the enemy or other sources that might be useful to our own cause. It is no part of censorship to suppress free speech or free criticism of persons or of the government; in no sense is that a function of censorship. I should not want to see any steps taken under the guise of censorship for the purpose of suppressing free criticism. Even during times of war there is real value in criticism.
I should like to advert to one unpleasant incident this evening, the quotation by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) of a letter which he had received from someone and which had been written in another part of the country. I think it is much to be regretted that letters of that sort should be even referred to in the House of Commons. That sort of discussion cannot possibly do any good to anyone here in Canada, particularly at this time when there is the utmost need for the people in one part of the country to be as moderate as they possibly can in their references to the people in another part of the country.
I should like to advert also to a statement made by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). Sometimes I feel that I am not as free as a minister of the crown as I was when I was a private member. As a private member I could state that I would pay no attention to the hon. member for Broadview, but as a minister I cannot take that attitude. I must pay some attention to him because of the fact that he represents a constituency. But time and time again he has sought to make a differentiation between Canadians of British origin and Canadians who are not of British origin. That differentiation ought not to be made by anyone at this time. We are all Canadians regardless of our origin, regardless of whether it is British, or French or neither British nor French. We are all in this war. We have earned rights in this country which carry with them corresponding duties. This is a conflict which touches every individual in this country, and it is not the time for differentiation between Canadians of various racial origins. We are all united in our devotion to Canada and in our devotion to the cause for which all Canadians fight. That cause can best be described as the cause of humanity.

Are we not devoted to the
empire?

We are deeply attached to our association with Great Britain and our sister dominions. The fact that we entered this war of our own accord does not lessen our attachment to Great Britain from which we
inherit the traditions and institutions that are so dear to every Canadian regardless of his origin. I take second place to no man in this country in my devotion to British institutions and British traditions. I plead with everyone in Canada that at this time there should be the utmost moderation in thought and speech and the greatest respect paid by one part of the country to all other parts of the country.

During the recent plebiscite the returning officers were appointed under authority of the minister, and I am sure that some of them must have notified the department of what happened in connection with the registration cards. Mr. Frank Saxon of Toronto writes me that perhaps twenty or thirty per cent of those presenting themselves to vote presented cards bearing addresses which were different from those at which the persons lived, they having moved since they first registered. Earlier in the afternoon the minister referred to the fact that in many instances it was found that men called up had moved from the addresses under which they had first registered. Mr. Saxon suggests that this difficulty would be overcome if these people could obtain new registration cards at local post offices. The new card could be of a different colour, and the original card would be returned to the department. The department would then have a complete and up-to-date record of the addresses of those who were registered. Has the minister had any report from his returning officers as to the effect of these people moving from their former addresses?

I think there have been a million and a half address changes. I have not had brought to my attention the facts that the hon. member for Davenport now brings to the attention of the committee, and I shall be glad to bring his observations to the attention of the appropriate officers who are in charge of the national registration records.

This afternoon the
minister stated that the age limit for call had been raised from thirty to thirty-five years.
No.
That it was intended to raise it shortly in some places.
I indicated that I would not be surprised if that step were taken in the near future.

At the same time the minister indicated that one reason for doing that was that in certain military districts the

War Appropriation-War Services
number of men within the age limits had been practically exhausted, and he referred particularly to military district No. 3 which is located at Kingston, Ontario. This strikes me as being a peculiar situation. The Department of National War Services is calling men within certain age limits, and I cannot understand why one particular military district should have its man-power within those age limits exhaust- ' ed so that the government may have to raise the classification in order to get the necessary quota of men from that district. I wonder if it is a case of all available men within that age class who can be taken from industry having been taken. If that is so, how does it come that in military district No. 3-
Administrative division C.

In administrative division "C", which is military district No. 3, the age has been raised from twenty-eight to thirty, which would indicate, at first sight at all events, that a heavier drain has been made on the available man-power in that area than in other areas in Canada.
Not necessarily.
Per se.

Not necessarily, the minister says, but I would ask how he can set aside that conclusion. In a particular area more men might possibly be drawn from nonessential war industries into essential war industries or into military service than in another area, but in that particular area we have the classification raised, or contemplated to be raised in order to get more men to fill the army quota-and that before even the lottery system has been embarked upon. Certainly it has every appearance of discrimination, if not in reality. It might very well be pointed out that enlistments in that particular area had so depleted the available man-power that a sufficient number of men were not available and that the government, in order to get more men, increased the age limit. I should like to hear an explanation from the minister.

It would not be possible, for a multiplicity of causes, for the reserves of man-power to be the same in all administrative divisions across Canada. I have not any doubt that part of the situation that exists in administrative division "C" is due to a very heavy volume of enlistments of a voluntary nature in that division. That was its record in the last war, and I think it is its record in this war. But that is only one cause.
Is that not the major cause?

Similarly the man-power reserve available for call in another area may be reduced by reason of the concentration of essential war industries in that area and the fact that a large number of postponements of military training have been granted to men essential to war industry. When I made the statement about administrative division "C", I indicated that we were coming close to exhaustion in that administrative division. I also indicated that we would within a very short time be coming close to exhaustion in a number of other divisions. I also indicated that we would be in a better position to know what the reserves of man-power were in other administrative divisions after we had seen the full impact of, let us say, the agricultural regulations and the man-power reserve in the various administrative divisions. As we move up into the higher age groups, the number of men who can be brought into the armed forces becomes smaller and smaller. I do not think I can go further at the moment.
One of the reasons for the situation in administrative division "C" has been enlistments. Another reason has been postponements of military training for one reason or another. There may be other reasons that do not occur to me at the moment.

I want to call the minister's attention to the fact that a serious attack was made here this evening by one of his own supporters on a division of his department, the bureau of public information.
I hold no brief for the director of that division. I recognize in him one of the ablest publicity men in Canada.
I did not understand that an attack was made on the director.

No, but on the department, and it has not brought any response or any defence from the minister. That, of course, is his business.
I wonder if the members of the house understand exactly what the position is. I have received from time to time, as I have no doubt every member of the house has, letters protesting against the character of some of the press releases and information that is being given out, particularly with respect to the length of time that has elapsed between the times of preparation and distribution of the material. I took this question up with Mr. Lash, and we had some interesting correspondence. I was surprised to learn that this was the position: There are about fifteen or sixteen or seventeen publicity men attached to various departments of government all more or less related to war work, not to speak of peace-time propagandists attached to

War Appropriation-War Services
various departments; this material prepared by this large number of press men, I learned, is sent in to the division of public information merely for, shall I say, distribution purposes, and the director has no authority to edit or alter one word of these releases. In other words, he is merely a conduit through which this information is distributed to the public. That is my understanding, and if that be so,
I think the position ought to be reviewed.
A man of the experience of Mr. Lash as a publicist, with a flair for news, I suppose, equal if not superior to that of any of the young pressmen attached to the various government departments, should have some authority to put the "can" on some of the material that is going out or to alter or refer it back. That is a constructive suggestion I * make to the minister. If my understanding of the position is correct-and I speak, of course, subject to correction-the present position ought to be reviewed. The bureau is working very hard, and I do not think at enormous expense. I had the figures once; I think they have been given to the house once or twice, and it is not an enormous expenditure. But through a misunderstanding I believe that the bureau of information is called upon to take some of the odium that properly belongs to the departments from whose officials the information emanates. I understand that the director of public information has no authority to refer back or even to edit the articles that are sent in to him. He must of necessity be just a distribution centre. I note that Mr. Lash has made some excellent radio broadcasts himself; I listen to them whenever the opportunity offers, which is not as often as I should like. He is an experienced man; that is why he is there. I have no doubt he was loaned to the government by the national railways because of his capability, and I do not think it is fair that the attack made on the bureau to-night should go unanswered. I do not like to see that type of incident happen, and I think the minister ought to do something with regard to it.
I rose merely because I had that thought, not to make a speech but to call attention to what developed here this evening, to give the committee my understanding of what the true position is, and to ask the minister to review the functions of this bureau with respect to the flow of material which must come to it from all these different sources. There are, I think, too many pressmen in the employ of the government. I have the idea that the newspapers of this country, if given a free hand, could do a much better job with respect to public information than all these
liaison officers in the departments. That is something which is worthy of consideration.
I know that there are newspaper men in Canada who hold that view. The government thinks it necessary to have all these men putting out miles and miles of propaganda, but the public know it is propaganda, and they discount a lot of it. It is not objective enough. It savours of propaganda, and the people do not believe all they read.

The leader of the opposition has suggested that I should reply to the attack made on the bureau of public information by the hon. member for Temiscouata. I do not know whether I should reply to everything the hon. member said.
Oh, I did not say that.
I had sent in to me just a little while ago a memorandum reading as follows: "Long distance competition in patience: first place, Thorson; honourable mention, Job".

What
about the members of this committee who have had to listen to it?

I have been waiting for someone to ask me for information with regard to the division of public information, which is one of the divisions under my charge. Most of the time that I have been before the committee the discussion has been on the division of mobilization, and has dealt with only one aspect of the mobilization division.
You have too many divisions.
I do not think so.
I do think so. The minister should have mobilization only.

Everyone is, of course,
entitled to his own opinion.
Well, that is enough for him.

I am delighted with the opportunity of indicating what the functions of the bureau of public information are, what its objectives are, and the manner in which it functions, but it would take some time. It cannot be done in just a few moments.
We want to get through this summer some time.

There is a great misunderstanding as to the particular function of the bureau of public information to which the
2964	COMMONS
War Appropriation-War Services
leader of the opposition has made reference. The bureau is not in competition with the daily press of Canada. It is not a function of that bureau to prepare official news announcements for the use of the daily press; not at all. All the daily newspapers of Canada have their news-gathering organizations; they have their representatives in the press gallery; they have their parliamentary correspondents in Ottawa; they are members of either the Canadian Press or the British United Press, and these news-gathering organizations send news to their member newspapers. The various news-gathering organizations get the news direct from the government departments. The spot news, as it is called, goes direct from the departments to the press gallery, to the Canadian Press, and to the British United Press. The bureau of public information, in so far as spot news is concerned, has very little to do with the daily newspapers. There are, however, a great many other functions which it has to perform and may quite properly perform. While the association between the bureau of public information and the daily newspapers is of comparatively small importance, the association between the bureau and the weekly newspapers is, on the other hand, much closer. The service which the bureau of public information can render to the weekly newspapers at their request is very much greater than it attempts to render to the daily newspapers, who have their own individual news-gathering organizations and set-ups.
The leader of the opposition referred to the fact that a great many men are engaged in publicity work of one kind or another, or public relations work of various kinds, in the departments. One of the purposes of the Department of National War Services was said to be, in the order in council which assigned that function to it, the coordination of existing sources of public information. There were in existence already publicity set-ups in the three departments of national defence; there were also publicity and public relations branches in the Department of Munitions and Supply and in a number of other departments of government. It has never been considered either possible or desirable that all agencies of either publicity, public relations or public information should come together exclusively in one department under one administration.
It was thought that greater success could be achieved in coordinating public relations and public information by a policy of cooperation than by an attempt to have everything go through one funnel. The manner in which the division of the bureau of public information has operated almost since the commencement, and certainly after I came into the 
department, was to follow that policy of coordination by cooperation rather than by regimentation. We established in a formal way last July an interdepartmental committee, which had operated in a more or less informal way previously. That interdepartmental committee is presided over by the Hon. T. C. Davis, one of my associate deputy ministers. It meets weekly with the representatives of publicity and of the various press organizations of the war departments and various other organizations. The following departments and organizations of government have representatives on this interdepartmental committee: the three departments of national defence; Department of Munitions and Supply; Department of Labour; wartime prices and trade board; national war finance committee; foreign exchange control board; Department of External Affairs; Canadian Broadcasting Corporation; national film board, and bureau of public information. I know exactly what will be said if I start to give a description of the bureau of public information; but I am handicapped again, as I have been previously, in that I have a request to explain the operations of a division of the department and then am told that I should do so in one or two words.

I did not invite the minister to cover the whole field. All I was bringing to his attention was a situation which I think at present exists and which needs correction. That is all I want him to talk about.

This interdepartmental
committee has served a useful purpose in coordinating public information.

I rise to refute a statement made by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). While speaking in a general way he indicated that Ontario was No. 1 in enlistment in the army, navy and air force.
I have here the best figures I have been able to obtain. They first appeared in a Toronto paper, and I am sure they would have been at least fair with Ontario. In these figures Ontario appears to be the sixth province down the line. I will give the number by provinces up to that point. These are per 10.000 of population. Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, taken together, give 495 persons as having joined the army, air force and navy- and I am talking about the active service. Manitoba is next with 490 persons; British Columbia third with 483; New Brunswick fourth with 428; Alberta fifth with 444; and Ontario not first, but sixth, with 426 persons

War Production
for every 10,000 of population. I wish to correct the hon. member for Broadview in that
regard.

The hon. member meant
in numbers.
What are the figures for the rest of the provinces?
Saskatchewan, 326; and Quebec, 204.

I have no desire to prolong the discussion, because I realize that the minister has been patient and long-suffering. Members of the committee could walk out at any time, but the minister could not. He has my sympathy. In the course of my remarks this afternoon I referred to representation on the boards. I still contend there is a necessity for a rearrangement of the personnel of the boards. My contention is that in the past they served a purpose. The board in Nova Scotia, with which we have had no quarrel in the past, consists at present of the Hon. Mr. Justice Doull of the supreme court, His Honour N. R. McArthur and His Honour K. L. Crowell, three judges. As I visualize the functions of these boards in the future it will require considerable moving around, because in my opinion most of the men who will be called for service in the future will come from the industries, and while the employer has the right to sit in and protect his interests-

speechtext: It is eleven o'clock.
May we not allow the hon. member to finish?

I shall be only a minute; I want the minister to answer a simple question. In the United States, in connection with the national selective service there, as outlined recently by the man in charge, there are community boards.
There are about 6,500.

Yes; and in the community there is no difficulty in making decisions. There is a large call-up from the industrial section now, and it is necessary for the board to sit. I visualize considerable difficulty in that connection, and I am wondering if the minister would not consider allowing on the boards representation from the labour unions. In the New Brunswick set-up the secretary of the federation of labour for New Brunswick sits on the board. Could that not be done in the other provinces? I think labour is entitled to a representative on the board. The employer has the right to go there; all the
others sit in judgment on whether or not a man is essential, except the man who is going to be taken. I do not say that each and every union should be represented, but I believe the provincial organizations, the federations and so on, should be entitled to representation on that board, as is the case in New Brunswick. I think before we go much further with this business of taking men from industries we are going to have to adopt the United States set-up if we want to have the system function properly. They are serving without remuneration; there is no cost; in my opinion the procedure is much quicker and the decisions much more practical, because the decisions are made by men who live right in the community and who know the conditions that exist. I think we shall have to consider adopting that system. Will the minister give consideration to the possibility of giving the working men representation on these boards?

That may well be given consideration, particularly in those districts or divisions in which there are large concentrations of war industries. I shall be very glad indeed to give further consideration to the suggestion of my hon. friend.
Progress reported.
It being five minutes after eleven o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
